Md Umair, the eldest son of Abdul Bari, 50, the prime accused in the rape case, filed the case with Savar Model Police Station today, naming six people and accusing another 10 to 15 unidentified individuals, said Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain, inspector (investigation) of the police station.

The case was filed over allegations of looting and vandalism at the madrasa, the inspector said.

According to the case statement, the accused looted Tk 47 lakh in cash, 12 bhori of gold ornaments worth Tk 23 lakh, and other valuables worth Tk 7 lakh from the madrasa.

Inspector Mosharraf said, “We had advised the madrasa authorities against naming the complainant in the rape case as an accused in the looting and vandalism case. However, the madrasa authorities intend to accuse him. We will not arrest him without an investigation.”

Md Umair, who described himself as the madrasa’s assistant administrator, told The Daily Star that the rape case against his father was false and fabricated. He alleged that false accusations had been brought against his father to grab the madrasa’s land and property and loot its assets.

Cash and gold ornaments worth Tk 77 lakh were looted from the madrasa, while the vandalism caused damage worth more than Tk 1 crore, he said.

Meanwhile, relatives of the rape victim expressed anger over the complainant in the rape case being named as an accused in the case over the madrasa looting and vandalism.

They also criticised the police for not yet arresting Abdul Bari.

According to police, on October 22, police arrested the wife of madrasa headteacher Maulana Md Ab Bari in Savar over allegations that she had abetted in the alleged rape of the 13-year-old student and threatened the victim into silence. Bari remains on the run. As news of the alleged rape spread, angry locals surrounded and vandalised the madrasa.
summary: Madrasa authorities allege Tk 77 lakh in cash and gold ornaments stolen

title: 2 cops injured in attack during procession 'in support of AL' in Gopalganj
body:
Two policemen were injured after a police van came under attack during a procession allegedly organised by Jubo League, whose activities are banned, and banned organisation Chhatra League in Gopalganj.

Two police personnel, including Sub-Inspector Ful Mia of Gopalganj Sadar Police Station, were injured in the incident, said its Officer-in-Charge (OC) Mohammad Aminul Islam.

The incident took place this afternoon in the Raghunathpur Kheya Ghat area of Gopalganj Sadar upazila.

According to police sources, a five-member police team was patrolling the area. At that time, SI Ful Mia and another police officer had stepped out of their vehicle and were standing on the road when suddenly, a flash procession came out from an alley and approached the police while chanting, “Sheikh Hasina will return! Bangladesh will smile!”

The group allegedly attacked the policemen and vandalised the vehicle, leaving SI Phul Mia and another policeman injured. Police were also chased by the people in the procession, police said.

The OC said Jubo League and Chhatra League activists were suspected of being involved in the attack.

He added, “We are investigating whether any influential individual or group instigated the incident. Police operations are underway to identify and arrest those involved.”
summary: Participants chant slogans in support of Sheikh Hasina; police investigate suspected Jubo League, Chhatra League involvement

title: Madrasa teacher sent to jail over alleged rape attempt in Pabna
body:
A Pabna court today sent a madrasa teacher to jail in a case filed over the alleged attempted rape of a student at a residential girls' madrasa in Pabna Sadar upazila on Thursday night.

Pabna Judicial Magistrate Court passed the order after police produced the accused, Abu Eusuf Pramanik, before it today, said Sanjoy Kumar Shaha, inspector (investigation) of Pabna Sadar Police Station.

He was arrested soon after the victim’s family filed a case over the alleged rape attempt, said the inspector.

According to police and locals, Abu Eusuf, director and residential teacher of the madrasa, had been teaching at the madrasa for the past five years. He allegedly attempted to rape the student on Thursday night, but she managed to escape and informed locals.

Angry locals went to the madrasa, caught the teacher and beat him up. Police went to the spot, rescued him and took him into custody early Friday.

The madrasa has 60 students, including 30 residential students. Police later rescued the residential students and handed them over to their parents.

However, enraged locals set fire to the madrasa building early Friday.
summary: Teacher accused of attempting to rape residential student; madrasa building later set on fire

title: Jubo Dal leader, grocery shop owner shot in Khulna
body:
Unidentified assailants shot a local Jubo Dal leader and a grocery shop owner in separate incidents in the Khulna district today.

In Terokhada upazila, Ramim Biswas, 32, president of Jubo Dal's ward-3 unit in Madhupur union, suffered a bullet wound in an armed attack around 11:10am in Parhaji village, confirmed Kabir Hossain, inspector (investigation) of Terokhada Police Station.

According to a press release issued by Khulna District Police, Ramim was sitting in a van in front of a house near Khan Bricks in Parhaji village, along the Sen-er Bazar-Madhupur Road. At that time, unidentified assailants on a motorcycle fired at him from behind and fled the scene. A bullet hit his rib cage.

In Khulna town, grocery shop owner Dhananjay Kundu alias Akash Kundu, 45, of Gachhtala Temple area, was shot on Dakshin Tutpara Cross Road around 6:45pm, said Khulna Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge of Lokmon Hossain.

Quoting eyewitnesses, the OC said the assailants arrived on a motorcycle, fired a single shot at Akash and fled the scene. Akash sustained a gunshot wound to his abdomen.

Both of them were rescued by locals and taken to Khulna Medical College Hospital.

The identities of the attackers and the motive behind the shootings were not immediately known, police said.

Security was beefed up following the shooting.

The incidents took place on the same day inspector general of police was on an official visit in the district.

Today, IGP Ali Hossain Fakir visited Khulna Police Lines to meet police personnel and representatives of different policing committees.

'Shootings mar Khulna district'

The shootings comes amid growing concerns over law and order in Khulna, where a series of killings and shooting incidents have marred the district all year.

According to district police data, 35 murders were reported in Khulna district between January and the first week of October this year. Police had solved 25 of the cases, while the remaining 10 were yet to be solved, Khulna Superintendent of Police Sarker Omar Faroque said earlier.

Meanwhile, Khulna Metropolitan Police (KMP) recorded 33 murders in the city between January and September. Police claimed to have solved 31 of the cases.

According to a police list, at least 10 major criminal gangs are active in Khulna city. Clashes, retaliatory attacks, and killings have occurred among these groups over territorial control and revenge.

Meanwhile, a joint force has launched a special operation in four upazilas of Khulna to improve law and order, with a focus on curbing drug-related crimes and recovering illegal firearms.

The operation began on October 6 in Rupsha, Dighalia, Terokhada and Batiaghata upazilas, involving the Special Response Battalion (SRB; formerly RAB), KMP, and district police.

“Most of the targeted killings in Khulna are linked to drug-related activities,” the SP told The Daily Star.
summary: The incidents took place on the same day inspector general of police was on an official visit in the district

title: Constable among three detained with yaba in Gazipur
body:
Police detained three people, including a police constable, with 120 yaba pills in Gazipur's Sreepur late last night.

The detainees are Constable Sarwar Murshed, 38, posted to the Traffic North Division of Gazipur Metropolitan Police; Md Sabuj, 32; and Md Jahangir Alam, 36.

They were detained at a house in the Keowa Purbakhanda area of Sreepur Municipality around 11:30pm yesterday after locals held them and informed police. Officers from Sreepur Police Station later went to the scene and detained the trio.

Mohammad Shahinur Alam, officer-in-charge of Sreepur Police Station, confirmed the information to The Daily Star this afternoon.

According to witnesses, Jahangir had been living in a rented room at the house for about a month.

They alleged that he had been running a drug business from the house, selling yaba and other narcotics.
summary: Locals held the trio at a house in Sreepur late Friday and alerted police

title: Road crash claims six more lives
body:
A toddler, her mother, and aunt were among six people who died after a bus rammed into an auto-rickshaw in Bakerganj, Barishal, yesterday afternoon.

One-and-a-half-year-old Farhana died at Sher-E-Bangla Medical College Hospital, her mother Shathi, 22, died on the way to the facility and aunt Tanjila, 30, died at the scene, police said, adding that the family is from Gaurnadi upazila of Barishal.

The other deceased are Bakerganj residents Sohag Shikder, 21, Hasib Khan, 25, and Amir Chowdhury, 50.

Two others injured in the crash are being treated at the hospital with serious injuries.

The bus of Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation, going towards Barishal from Kuakata, was on the wrong side of the road when it collided with the auto-rickshaw coming from the opposite direction.

The crash happened in front of a fire service office, said Bakerganj Upazila Nirbahi Officer Sajal Chandra Shil, adding that the driver managed to flee the scene.

Alauddin Milan, officer-in-charge of Bakerganj Police Station, said the auto-rickshaw got completely mangled in the impact.

Shah Alam, assistant director at Bangladesh Road Transport Authority office in Barishal, said the bus had no fitness certificate since May 28, 2015, and its registration expired towards the end of 2017.

"We cannot say anything about the driver because we do not have the identity of the driver. We are searching for information on the driver," he told The Daily Star.
summary: A toddler, her mother, and aunt were among six people who died after a bus rammed into an auto-rickshaw in Bakerganj, Barishal, yesterday afternoon.

title: Rajapaksa ally elected Lanka president
body:
Six-time prime minister Ranil Wickremesinghe was elected as crisis-wracked Sri Lanka's new president by the country's parliament yesterday, with the backing of the party of the ex-leader -- who fled abroad after his palace was stormed by protesters.

Official results showed Wickremesinghe garnered 134 votes in the 225-member parliament, with his main opponent Dullas Alahapperuma getting 82 and leftist Anura Dissanayake just three, giving him an absolute majority on first preferences.

"Our country is facing massive challenges and we have to work on a new strategy to fulfil the aspirations of the people," the 73-year-old leader said after his victory. "Now everyone must come together."

He will be sworn in this morning and will appoint a new prime minister within the course of the day, officials from the President's Office told Xinhua.

He is expected to name public administration minister Dinesh Gunawardena, 73, his schoolmate and a strong Rajapaksa loyalist, as the new prime minister.

Wickremesinghe takes charge of a bankrupt nation that is in bailout talks with the IMF, with its 22 million people enduring severe shortages of food, fuel and medicine.

But he was backed by the Rajapaksas' SLPP party -- still the largest in parliament -- and is despised as a proxy for the former leader by the protesters who forced him from his palace after months of demonstrations over the unprecedented economic crisis.

On the streets, the mood was sombre. Soon after the election result was announced, a burst of chants broke out against Wickremesinghe. It lasted only a few minutes, before the small group of protesters left the steps of the secretariat.

But some vowed to keep up their protest against the 73-year-old leader.

Civil engineer Nuzly Hameem said he was "disappointed" by the result. "We expected more from our parliamentarians," he told AFP.

The protests would "obviously" continue, he said, but added "We are burnt out. It's been four months."

"The reason why people came out against Gota(baya) was not a personal grudge. It was protesting for ideals and values he held," said Buwanaka Perera, a 26-year-old protester.

"We see those same values, corruption and oppression in Ranil."

Wickremesinghe has pledged to crack down hard if protesters take to the streets and hundreds of heavily armed troops and police stood guard outside the parliament, but there were no signs of demonstrators.

As acting president, Wickremesinghe extended a state of emergency that gives police and security forces sweeping powers, and last week ordered troops to evict protesters from state buildings they had occupied.

A court yesterday ordered the protesters to vacate their camp near the Presidential Secretariat and confine themselves only to an area designated as a protest site.

Opposition MP Dharmalingam Sithadthan said ahead of the vote that Wickremesinghe's hardline stance against demonstrators had gone down well with MPs who had been at the receiving end of mob violence, describing him as the "law-and-order candidate".

Wickremesinghe automatically became acting president when Rajapaksa resigned and political analyst Kusal Perera said he had "regained the acceptance of the urban middle classes by restoring some of the supplies like gas and he has already cleared government buildings showing his firmness".

But he appears to be indebted to the Rajapaksas, a clan of four brothers who have dominated Sri Lankan politics for much of the last two decades, for his victory.

Gotabaya's departure wounded the group after two of his brothers also quit their posts as premier and finance minister earlier this year.

But former president Mahinda Rajapaksa, the deposed Gotabaya's elder brother and the head of the family, remained in the country, and party sources said he had pressed SLPP legislators to support Wickremesinghe.
summary: Six-time prime minister Ranil Wickremesinghe was elected as crisis-wracked Sri Lanka’s new president by the country’s parliament yesterday, with the backing of the party of the ex-leader -- who fled abroad after his palace was stormed by protesters.

title: ‘If money is coming from across the border, why are you in government?’: Shafiqur
body:
Leader of the Opposition and Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Shafiqur Rahman has warned that attempts to implement the July Charter through constitutional amendments could be struck down by the courts, urging instead that reforms be carried out in line with the referendum verdict.

“If you amend it again, a court will completely whitewash it. We are not accustomed to following this futile path and repeating the mistakes of the past,” he said at a discussion organised by Jamaat at the National Press Club in Dhaka to mark the first anniversary of the signing of the July Charter.

“The ‘No’ vote was swept away by people's aspirations, and 70 percent voted ‘Yes’. The people have made it clear that they no longer want to see the rotten, outdated politics of the past. We want change and reforms,” he said.

Referring to the special committee formed to amend the constitution, Shafiqur said the opposition was being asked to join a process that could leave the referendum verdict unimplemented. He argued that the existing constitution had not only given birth to fascism but had also sought to make it permanent.

“The government will be bound to implement this referendum verdict,” he said, adding that Jamaat would continue its movement to establish people's rights rather than pursue party-specific demands.

Shafiqur also responded to remarks made by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in Rajshahi on October 20, when the premier alleged that the ousted regime was sending money from across the border to a political party accused of spreading misinformation and trying to create instability.

“If money is coming from across the border, why are you in government? Why can’t you stop it from entering the country?” Shafiqur said, also questioning the government’s failure to prevent weapons and drugs from being smuggled across the border.

“A government that is incapable of preventing such unwanted activities has no right to govern the country,” he added.

Leaders of the Jamaat-led 11-party alliance also spoke at the discussion.
summary: Opposition leader hits back at PM Tarique’s claim of cross-border funding aimed at creating instability

title: Outsiders restricted in Thakurgaon-1 ahead of October 29 by-polls
body:
The EC has ordered all outsiders to stay out of Thakurgaon-1 constituency from 8:00am on October 27 to 4:00pm on October 30 ahead of the by-election scheduled for October 29.

The EC sent a letter to the Thakurgaon deputy commissioner and superintendent of police today, directing them to take the necessary steps to enforce the directive.

According to the letter, the commission has decided that only election officials, individuals authorised by the EC, and residents or voters of the constituency will be allowed to remain in the electoral area from 48 hours before voting begins until 24 hours after voting ends.

As a result, all outsiders must leave the constituency within the stipulated period, the letter said.

The EC said the measure aims to ensure that the election to the vacant Thakurgaon-1 parliamentary seat is held in a free, fair and peaceful manner, without undue influence.
summary: Restrictions will remain in force from 8:00am on October 27 until 4:00pm on October 30 to ensure a free, fair election, says EC

title: Next election under caretaker govt after constitutional amendment: Salahuddin
body:
The next national election will be held under a caretaker government, with the system restored through a constitutional amendment, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said today.

“Of course, the next election will be held under a caretaker government,” he said during a press briefing at the Home Ministry this afternoon.

He said political consensus had already been reached on the issue. Referring to the Supreme Court’s decision on the 13th Amendment, Salahuddin said the court had overturned the earlier judgment by Justice Khairul Haque and judicially revived the caretaker government system. However, a constitutional amendment would be required to formally restore it.

“We are committed to this. Restoring the caretaker government system was one of the demands of our movement,” he said.

Asked about social media reports that ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina might return to Bangladesh in December, Salahuddin said the government had also heard the claims.

Bangladesh had sent several requests to India through the Foreign Ministry seeking her return under the extradition treaty, he said.

“Our stance is clear,” he added.

Asked whether developments surrounding her reported return could create instability, the home minister accused forces associated with the ousted regime of continuing their efforts to destabilise the country.

“We will not allow anyone to create instability in Bangladesh,” he said, adding that attempts by what he described as fallen forces or fugitives to create unrest would not be tolerated.

Regarding the attack on police in Gopalganj, Salahuddin said members of the political activity-banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations, including Chhatra League and Jubo League, had attempted to hold a procession near a ferry terminal in a union of Gopalganj Sadar.

A small police patrol sent to the spot came under attack, he said, adding that the authorities had reviewed video footage and were taking action against those involved.

On Sajek, the minister said the law and order situation had been brought under control. He said several groups, including the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti and the United People’s Democratic Front and their factions, had been involved in internal disputes and attempts to establish control over different areas during the tourism season.

The government and Bangladesh Army had taken measures to maintain law and order, while discussions with local leaders and headmen were continuing, he added.

Asked about allegations against an additional deputy inspector general of police over a raid at his house in Purbachol, Salahuddin said the officer had been attached and departmental proceedings would be initiated.

“We will follow all legal procedures. We will not consider anyone’s identity,” he said.

Salahuddin said Durga Puja had been celebrated peacefully and safely, amid communal harmony and with enthusiasm, across the country after many years.

He thanked law enforcement agencies, intelligence organisations, journalists and people from all walks of life for their cooperation.

The government had taken preventive measures rather than waiting for incidents to occur, he said.
summary: Home minister warns against attempts to destabilise the country, hails peaceful Durga Puja celebrations

title: Home minister busy with every ministry but his own - Alleges Shafiqur
body:
Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer and Leader of the Opposition Shafiqur Rahman yesterday criticised Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed for allegedly interfering in other ministries’ affairs while failing to maintain law and order.

“Fortunately, we got such a home minister. He serves in all ministries. He neither controlled drugs nor weapons, nor was he able to restore law and order in the country,” he told reporters at Moulvibazar Circuit House yesterday morning.

Shafiqur was on his first organisational visit to his home district of Moulvibazar since the national elections.

He said the home ministry was among the most sensitive and critical ministries, and its effective functioning was essential to maintaining law and order.

However, he alleged that Salahuddin had failed to manage his own ministry and was interfering in education, health and local government affairs, which he described as contrary to good governance.

The opposition leader claimed that law and order had effectively broken down, with incidents of murder, rape, extortion and illegal land grabbing increasing daily.

He also alleged that the police administration was being used for partisan purposes.

Condemning corruption and extortion, Shafiqur said those involved in such activities did not truly belong to any political party and ultimately harmed themselves and their parties. Such individuals, he said, were the first to flee when their parties faced crises.

He also pledged to play an active role in parliament to improve infrastructure, educational institutions and healthcare services in Moulvibazar.
summary: Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer and Leader of the Opposition Shafiqur Rahman yesterday criticised Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed for allegedly interfering in other ministries’ affairs while failing to maintain law and order.

title: Youth gets 7-day remand over Facebook ‘sniper’ comment on PM Tarique’s Rajshahi visit
body:
A Dhaka court today placed a youth on seven-day remand in a case filed over a Facebook comment that said “only a sniper was missing,” referring to a bus used to transport Prime Minister Tarique Rahman during his visit to Rajshahi.

Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Sarah Farzana Haque passed the order in the case filed under the Anti-Terrorism Act after Detective Branch (DB) of police produced Abu Bokor Siddique, 22, before the court with a seven-day remand prayer

Additional Public Prosecutor Muhammad Shamsud Doha Sumon confirmed the information.

On October 20, PM Tarique arrived at Shah Makhdum Airport in Rajshahi aboard a military aircraft around 3:00pm. He travelled from the airport to the city on a Rajshahi University of Engineering and Technology (RUET) bus, which he also used to attend a rally at the historic Madrasa Ground and visit Dharmasabha Mandir ahead of Durga Puja. He later returned to the airport on the same bus.

A Facebook page named “The Beauty of Rajshahi” posted a photograph of the bus. In the comments section, Abu Bokor wrote, “What a missed opportunity! Only a sniper was missing.”

According to a police forwarding report submitted to the court, the DB detected Abu Bokor’s comment on October 21.

The same day, Abu Bokor was detained in Paba upazila of Rajshahi.

“During initial questioning, the accused reportedly admitted to making the comment. Moreover, police recovered a mobile phone from his possession,” said the forwarding report.

On October 23, police filed the case with Ramna Police Station against Abu Bokor.
summary: Police say Abu Bokor Siddique made the Facebook remark about a bus used during the prime minister’s Rajshahi visit

title: Tongi madrasa teacher denied bail over alleged sexual abuse of 7-year-old student
body:
A Gazipur court today rejected the bail petition of Moslem Uddin, the vice-principal of a madrasa in Tongi, over allegations of sexually harassing and molesting a seven-year-old student.

Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court in Gazipur passed the order after hearing the bail petition submitted earlier in the day.

Court Inspector Ahsan Ullah Chowdhury confirmed the matter to The Daily Star this afternoon.

Investigation officer Ziaur Rahman told The Daily Star that the case was filed with Tongi West Police Station on October 22 under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act, 2000, incorporating the amended provisions introduced in 2025.

The accused was serving as vice-principal of Qariul Quran International Madrasa in the Madhya Auchpara area of Tongi.
summary: A Gazipur court today rejected the bail petition of Moslem Uddin, the vice-principal of a madrasa in Tongi, over allegations of sexually harassing and molesting a seven-year-old student

title: Tenant dies after landlord allegedly hits him with stick over rent dispute in Khulna
body:
A tenant died after his landlord allegedly struck him on the head with a stick following a dispute over rent in Basupara area of Khulna city.

The victim, Rakibul Islam, 24, died while undergoing treatment at Khulna Medical College Hospital this morning.

He was allegedly struck in the head by his landlord Majlis Khan, 82, during an argument yesterday, Sonadanga Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Rafiqul Islam told The Daily Star.

The body was kept at the hospital morgue for an autopsy and would be handed over to the family afterwards, he added.

Majlis has been detained in connection with the incident, but no case had been filed yet, the OC said.

According to police and local residents, an argument broke out between Rakibul and Majlis over rent at Shatarupa intersection in the Bakultala area of Basupara around 7:30pm yesterday.

At one stage, Majlis allegedly hit Rakibul on the head with a stick, leaving him injured.

Locals took Rakibul to KMCH, where he died this morning while receiving treatment.
summary: Landlord detained, but no case filed yet, police say

title: 2 killed in 'mob beating' over suspected auto-rickshaw theft in Rangpur
body:
Two men were beaten to death reportedly by a group of people over the alleged theft of a battery-powered auto-rickshaw in Gangachara upazila of Rangpur early today.

The deceased were identified as Ejarul Haque alias Rezaul Kana, 46, of Kachua Sardarpara village, and Sadikul Islam, 25, of Kolkond union in Gangachara, said police.

The incident took place in the Pukur Khurir Dola canal area of Bagpur Bagherhat village under Barabil union.

Abdus Sabur, officer-in-charge of Gangachara Model Police Station, said after recovering the bodies they were taken to the police station.

The bodies would be sent to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for autopsies to determine the exact cause of death.

“According to preliminary information from local residents, the two men died in a mob beating following the alleged theft of the auto-rickshaw,” the OC said.

According to police and locals, Sohel Mia, a resident of Bagpur Bagherhat village, noticed someone taking an auto-rickshaw from his house early today. He raised the alarm, prompting an announcement over the loudspeaker of a nearby mosque calling out, “Thief, thief.”

Hearing the announcement, local residents, including people who had gathered for Fajr prayers, chased the two men taking away the auto-rickshaw.

At one point, the men left the vehicle on the road and tried to flee. But locals caught them in a paddy field at Pukur Khurir Dola in the Uttar Panapukur area, about half a kilometre west of Sohel Mia’s house. They were then beaten, and both died at the scene.
summary: Locals chased the two men after a mosque loudspeaker announcement about the alleged theft

title: Man shot before hijacking motorcycle in Noakhali
body:
A tailor was shot, and his motorcycle hijacked in Begumganj upazila of Noakhali yesterday afternoon. However, the motorcycle was later recovered.

Locals rescued the victim, Kamrul Hasan, 24, of Newazpur, and took him to the 250-bed Noakhali General Hospital.

The shooting took place around 5:30pm in Ward 5 of Baro Newazpur village over a previous rivalry, Additional Superintendent of Police (Begumganj Circle) ANM Imran Khan said.

“The bullet entered through his right arm and grazed the skin of his abdomen, causing minor injuries. Police are investigating the matter and trying to identify the culprits and bring them to justice,” he told The Daily Star.

Mahbub Kabir, inspector (investigation) and acting officer-in-charge of Begumganj Police Station, said police visited the scene after receiving the information and recovered the motorcycle.

Legal action would be taken upon receipt of a formal complaint regarding the shooting, he added.

According to the victim's family and locals, Hasan works as a tailor in Chattogram and returned home on leave two days ago. Yesterday afternoon, he was riding a motorcycle with his cousin Rakib towards Bahadurpur village in Alaiyapur Union to meet an acquaintance.

When they reached the road in front of their house, a group intercepted them. At one point, one of the group opened fire, injuring Hasan in his right arm and the right side of his chest, the sources said.

Dr Rajib Ahmed Chowdhury, resident medical officer at the hospital, said Hasan was admitted around 7:00pm.

“He has a bullet injury on his arm. There is another bullet-like injury on the upper part of his abdomen, though no bullet was found there. He is currently undergoing treatment and is out of danger,” he said.
summary: Motorbike was later recovered, police say

title: Man beaten to death on theft suspicion in Pabna
body:
A young man was beaten to death by locals on suspicion of being a thief in Sujanagar upazila of Pabna early today.

The victim, identified as Sagor Sheikh alias Masud Rana, 25, of Hasampur village in the same upazila, worked as a rickshaw-van puller and carpenter, police said.

Quoting locals, Md Khoim Uddin, officer-in-charge of Sujanagar Police Station, said Rana was suspected of being a cattle thief when he was seen roaming near a house in Tantiband area around dawn. Locals chased him and caught him near Tantiband rail station, where he was beaten to death around 5:00am.

On information, police recovered the body and sent it to Pabna General Hospital morgue for autopsy.

The OC said no previous record of theft cases against Rana was found immediately.

Police are investigating the incident, and preparations are underway to file a case, the OC added.
summary: No previous record of theft cases against victim found immediately, say police

title: 556 tonnes of food grains missing from govt warehouse in Kurigram
body:
The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has found 556 tonnes of food grains missing from a government warehouse in Kurigram’s Sadar upazila.

The missing stock includes 521 metric tonnes of paddy and 35 metric tonnes of rice, said Sabdarur Islam, assistant director of the ACC’s Kurigram district office.

The finding was made during a day-long drive conducted today at the food warehouse located in the New Railway Station area.

Following the detection of the large-scale shortage, the ACC immediately sealed the warehouse, Sabdarur said.

The officer-in-charge of the facility failed to provide any satisfactory explanation for the missing rice and paddy, he said.

During the operation, the ACC team also found a quantity of rice that was unfit for human consumption.

“We are investigating how much more food grain in the warehouse is unfit for consumption,” the ACC official said.

He further added that preparations are underway to initiate legal action against the accused warehouse official in accordance with the law.

Kurigram District Food Controller Kazi Mohammad Hamidul Haque told The Daily Star on Sunday, “A departmental inquiry will be launched against the accused officer, Sharif Ahmed, and necessary departmental action will be taken.”

He also confirmed that the matter has already been reported to the higher authorities.
summary: ACC seals the warehouse

title: CID files money laundering case against ex-law minister Anisul Huq and associates
body:
Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has filed a money laundering case against former law minister Anisul Huq, his associate Toufika Karim, and two others over allegations of extortion amounting to Tk 24.53 crore.

According to preliminary findings of the CID’s Financial Crime Unit, Anisul Huq, Toufika Karim, Md Rashedul Kawsar Bhuiyan alias Jibon, and Md Kamruzzaman allegedly formed an "organised criminal ring" that systematically collected large sums of money through extortion over several years.

The details were shared in a press release signed by Jasim Uddin Khan, special superintendent (media) of CID.

Investigators said the group collected Tk 10 lakh monthly from individuals and organisations through the Gulshan branch of the National Bank of Pakistan. Kamruzzaman, who joined the bank as managing director in 2015, allegedly transferred money regularly to Toufika Karim’s personal account under the guise of a consultancy agreement with her law firm, Sirajul Haq Associates.

Until fleeing on August 5, 2024, the group reportedly collected Tk 10.80 crore from the National Bank of Pakistan alone.

The CID also found evidence of another Tk 10.60 crore deposited into Toufika Karim’s personal account from various individuals and organisations.

The investigation further revealed that after becoming law minister, Anisul Huq appointed Toufika Karim and Jibon as his personal secretaries and established an NGO named “Legal Assistance to Helpless Prisoner and Persons.”

In the NGO, Toufika served as chairperson, Jibon as secretary general, and Anisul himself as treasurer.

Using an account at Sonali Bank PLC’s Supreme Court branch, the group allegedly collected extortion money regularly. Between March 11, 2015, and June 30, 2024, a total of Tk 24.53 crore was collected through the NGO.

During the investigation, 26 bank accounts in Toufika Karim’s name containing Tk 24.53 crore were frozen following an order of the Dhaka Metropolitan Special Judge’s Court.
summary: 26 bank accounts containing Tk 24.53 crore frozen amid ongoing investigation

title: Musabbir murder likely linked to business dispute, says DB
body:
Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police has said the murder of Mohammad Azizur Rahman Musabbir, former general secretary of Dhaka City North Swechchhasebak Dal, appears to have stemmed from a business dispute.

At a press briefing at the DMP Media Centre this afternoon, Additional Commissioner (DB) Md Shafiqul Islam outlined the progress of the investigation, confirming that several suspects have been arrested during operations across Dhaka, Gazipur, Mymensingh, Netrokona, and Kishoreganj.

Among those detained are Jinnat, 24, one of the two gunmen, and Mohammad Billal Hossain, alleged to be the main coordinator of the attack.

Billal’s uncle, Abdul Kadir, 28, who reportedly helped the suspects flee, was also taken into custody.

Another suspect, Mohammad Riaz, 32, believed to have assisted in the planning, has been arrested as well.

Police recovered a motorcycle used in the attack and Tk 6,000 in cash from the suspects.

The second shooter, identified as Rahim, remains at large.

The DB official said the accused had inspected the crime scene prior to the attack. During initial questioning, the detainees confessed to their roles in the murder, though the firearm used in the shooting has not yet been recovered.

He added that while political motives are being examined given Musabbir’s background, initial findings suggest the killing was linked to a business dispute.

The DB is also investigating reports that Tk 1.5 million was allegedly sent from abroad to finance the killing.

Authorities are further examining a recent human chain staged by Musabbir against extortion, during which clashes occurred and a case was filed.

The incident took place last Wednesday around 8:00pm, when gunmen shot Musabbir in an alley near Hotel Super Star on Kazi Nazrul Islam Avenue.

Abu Sufian Bepari Masud, general secretary of the Tejgaon Thana Van Workers Union, who was accompanying Mosabbir, was also injured.
summary: Several suspects arrested across districts as police probe foreign funding angle

title: Right to privacy and non-consensual filming of citizens
body:
You are sitting with friends at a tea stall, walking through a market, or enjoying a concert or movie when you realise someone nearby is filming. A few hours later, you are in a video with a loud caption, and the comment section has already decided who you are. This has now become a common scenario in Bangladesh.

The rise of social media monetisation in recent years has made this practice increasingly visible. Formal journalists and broadcasters must follow the National Broadcasting Policy 2014, which restricts defamatory content, misleading information, and violations of personal privacy. However, the same standards rarely apply to self-proclaimed vloggers and content creators who record strangers without consent. Women, in particular, suffer the most, as their images are frequently used for sensational content and public scrutiny.

This normalisation of digital harassment usually rests on one argument: there is no privacy in public. However, the modern legal jurisprudence draws a crucial distinction between incidental observation and targeted fixation. The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), in multiple judgments, has recognised that even in public places, people have a ‘zone of interaction’ with others that is protected as part of their private life. In Von Hannover v Germany (2004), it ruled that filming someone merely to satisfy public curiosity, which adds nothing to a genuine public debate, may violate the right to privacy.

Similarly, when you enter a tea stall, you accept that people around you can see you. However, you do not automatically consent to your face being recorded, captioned, and permanently displayed to thousands of strangers. The United Nations Human Rights Committee, in General Comment No. 16 on Article 17 of the ICCPR, to which Bangladesh is a party, similarly states that individuals must be protected from arbitrary interference with their privacy, honour and reputation. Privacy, therefore, includes a degree of control over how personal information and images are used. These protections are also reflected in our Constitution. Article 32 protects life and personal liberty, while Article 43 recognises privacy (although to a certain extent), and Article 39 allows free speech subject to reasonable restrictions.

Moreover, existing laws already provide remedies against harmful digital conduct. Publishing an accusation meant to damage someone’s reputation is defamation under sections 499 and 500 of the Penal Code, and calling a woman unchaste may fit that squarely. Next, section 509 punishes words, gestures, or acts that insult a woman’s modesty or intrude on her privacy. Threatening to publish or share private content can amount to criminal intimidation under section 506. Penalties go up when images or videos are edited for sexual harassment. Making or sharing morphed sexual images, AI-generated sexual content, or doctored intimate videos can be punished under section 8 of the Pornography Control Act 2012 and section 25 of the Cyber Protection Act 2026. Both aim at digital content used to harm, threaten, or harass a person.

If this happens to you, save the evidence first: screenshots, links, the page name, dates, and comments. Then report the content to the platform. After that, go to the police station and file a general diary entry or a case. If the police refuse to act, you can file a complaint petition directly with a magistrate. You can also request the police to seek removal of the content through the National Cyber Protection Agency. Under section 8 of the Cyber Protection Act 2026, law enforcement agencies can ask the BTRC to block harmful content through the agency’s Director General. You can ask the court or tribunal handling your case to order the content removed as well. Cyber Tribunals hear online offences, and women and children repression tribunals hear the relevant cases.

If newspapers, online portals, or TV channels later publish a clip, you can file complaints with the relevant authorities. Complaints against broadcasters can be sent to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, while complaints against newspapers and news agencies can be filed with the Bangladesh Press Council under the Press Council Act 1974. However, these remedies apply only to media outlets, not individuals posting content on their own platforms.

Civil remedies also remain available but are rarely used. A person affected by harmful publication may seek damages through a defamation suit or request an injunction to remove the content. Where authorities fail to act, a writ petition under Article 102 may seek judicial directions for appropriate action.

For immediate danger, call 999. The government’s free 24/7 helpline 109 provides guidance on violence against women and children, including cyber abuse, while legal aid is available through 16430.

However, these remedies often come into play only after the victim has already suffered harm. The bigger challenge is holding unregulated content creators accountable for recording, sharing, and profiting from people’s private moments. Therefore, we urgently need a regulatory framework that distinguishes genuine mobile journalism from exploitative content creation.

Sharmista Banik is an intern at the Law Desk, the Daily Star.
summary: You are sitting with friends at a tea stall, walking through a market, or enjoying a concert or movie when you realise someone nearby is filming.
author: S Sharmista Banik

title: How ADR can  play a bigger role in criminal cases
body:
An agreement of 9 lakh taka has not stopped the legal controversy and the case around the recent Baridhara road crash. A 17-year-old boy accused of driving the car that killed construction worker Mehedi Hasan Mim was refused bail by a Dhaka juvenile court on 4 October. A report forwarded by the police to the court says investigators reviewed CCTV footage of the scene and surrounding areas, and it shows that the teenager was involved. The case brings up a question: when can a criminal case be settled by an agreement between the people involved, and when should the State continue with the trial?

In the civil justice system of Bangladesh, Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) is firmly embedded in the form of mediation, arbitration, and conciliation, especially in sections 89A to 89E of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. But its application in the criminal justice system is not so widespread. However, delays due to case backlogs, shortage of judges, and problems of obtaining witness evidence should prompt one to wonder whether ADR can play a bigger role in criminal cases as well.

Compounding of offences, as per section 345 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, is a significant form of criminal ADR. Compounding implies a compromise arrangement between the alleged victim and the accused to terminate the criminal procedure. However, simply because the two parties wish the criminal proceeding to end does not make it legal.

Section 345 identifies offences that may be compounded. In general, there are two categories: section 345(1) lists offences that are compoundable without the permission of the court, and section 345(2) deals with offences that require the court’s permission. Offences with a clear public element cannot automatically be converted into private offences simply because some form of compensation has been made. Under Section 345(6), lawful compounding results in the acquittal of the accused person with whom the offence is compounded.

The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh also recognised the importance of compromise within the statutory framework in Md Joynal v Md Rustom Ali (1984). The case is frequently cited in discussions of compromise as a form of ADR.

Coming back to the Baridhara case, the action was brought under sections 98 and 105 of the Road Transport Act, 2018. Section 117 of the 2018 Act makes the offences mentioned under sections 66, 72, 75, 87, 89 and 92 compoundable, while sections 98 and 105 are not compoundable. Hence, I believe even when the relatives of the deceased accept Tk 9 lakh voluntarily, the private compromise cannot end the proceeding.

However, the punishment provided under sections 98 and 105 is noteworthy as well. Section 98 provides imprisonment for a term which shall not exceed three years, or a fine not exceeding Tk 3 lakh, or both, and such fine may be paid in whole or in part to the aggrieved party by the court. Under section 105, an offender is liable to imprisonment for a term which shall not exceed five years, or a fine not exceeding Tk 5 lakh, or both. The reason behind considering the settlement of Tk 9 lakh as an ADR issue may be that the said settlement is above the maximum limit of fine prescribed in both the sections. The question thus arises whether there exists any mechanism within the legal system which can allow this allegedly voluntary settlement on the part of the victims’ family?

However, this is not to suggest that such issues can simply be swept aside. For Bangladesh, there could be a system where a judge ensures that compensation, consent, and the interests of the victim are considered while giving the government the right to ensure that the state interest is also protected. This discussion has become pertinent considering the amendment made in the Code of Criminal Procedure in 2026. Section 345(8) lays out that the court has the power to help in the compounding of compoundable offences when both parties agree to do so or refer the matter to the Legal Aid Officer or advocates. Such an agreement can be put on record and can be executed provided the rights of third parties are safeguarded.

It is also possible that Bangladesh may introduce a plea-bargaining scheme, which will be properly regulated. Contrary to compounding, plea bargaining will involve the acceptance of guilt in exchange for some legal bargain. Some examples of plea bargaining include charge bargaining, sentence bargaining, and fact bargaining, but it should be done very cautiously.

There is a need for criminal ADR in Bangladesh that should neither be dismissed completely nor considered without any caution. There is a need for a system in Bangladesh through which the minor crimes that deserve it can be disposed of through an efficient system, but the serious crimes must continue to attract public accountability. It is important for the courts to ensure that such agreements are made voluntarily, the parties are informed, and the agreements are legal, especially when vulnerable crime victims are forced to accept money. Only with sufficient safeguards in place will such a system work.

Ashraful Islam Plabon is a law student at Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP).
summary: An agreement of 9 lakh taka has not stopped the legal controversy and the case around the recent Baridhara road crash. A 17-year-old boy accused of driving the car that killed construction worker Mehedi Hasan Mim was refused bail by a Dhaka juvenile court on 4 October.
author: A Ashraful Islam Plabon

title: Dhaka’s traffic chaos:  Why fair enforcement is essential to law’s existence
body:
Dhaka is the noisy, chaotic capital of Bangladesh. Whenever you go out for a walk, you will always find its footpaths occupied by hawkers, often illegally, without having to pay any legal fee. A formal shopkeeper, in contrast, has to obtain trade permission, pay rents, taxes, and utility bills for carrying on his business in commercial spaces. Similarly, it is all the more convenient to park a car on the street illegally than to find a legal parking spot, which costs you money. The unfit buses emitting black smoke often get away with their non-compliance, whereas the fit ones have to bear the cost of renovation, production of fitness certificates, etc. These scenes appear far too common. But rarely do we ask what led the city to fall into such disarray.

The recent advent of e-rickshaws makes the asymmetry more apparent. While a licensed vehicle owner has to face legal hurdles for violating the traffic rules, the same does not apply to the unlicensed, unregulated e-rickshaws. With weak brakes, high speeds, and a lack of control, they often imperil the lives of pedestrians, especially children on the streets. Seeing all these irregularities and asymmetric application of law, one may be tempted to breach the law rather than to comply with it. Anarchy in Dhaka thus seems the natural conclusion for rational actors.

This apparent chaos in Dhaka can be explained using HLA Hart’s concept of sanction. Hart was one of the most influential legal theorists of the last century. In his magnum opus ‘The Concept of Law’, in which he developed his own theory of legal positivism, Hart devoted a significant portion of the book to critiquing Austin, one of the earliest proponents of legal positivism. Austin defined law as the command of the sovereign backed by sanction. By sanction, he meant the pain or punishment inflicted upon a person in case of non-compliance with a sovereign command. Its purpose is to provide the motivation for abiding by law. Without a sanction, there can be no command; without command, there can be no law at all. Thus, sanction plays an essential role in Austin’s legal theory.

Contrarily, Hart showed that sanction is not always necessary for the existence of law since people may obey the law, not out of fear of harm, but out of respect for the authority or being morally obliged. But Hart discovered something more to it. Despite being a legal positivist, who viewed law merely as a system of rules devoid of moral content, Hart conceded that a few rules of conduct must exist in order for any community to survive. They have their foundations in the human condition itself and are thus named as ‘the minimum content of natural law.’ These are derived from the five truisms about ourselves: (1) we are all vulnerable to each other, (2) we are approximately equal in powers, (3) we are selfish (limited altruism), in general, (4) we have limited resources, (5) we suffer from limited understanding and strength of will.

These limitations necessitate the formulation of some rules for the protection of life and property. However, the fifth truism is particularly useful to explain the situation in Dhaka. Because of our limitations in the understanding of the world along with our limited strength of will, we are often tempted to pursue our own immediate interests without considering their far-reaching consequences. This requires the establishment of social organisations for detecting and punishing them (sanction), without which many would succumb to such temptations.

Notably, the sanction Hart refers to here is different from the one Austin developed. According to Hart, the object of punishment (sanction) is not to supply the motive for obedience but to serve as a ‘guarantee that those who would voluntarily obey shall not be sacrificed to those who would not’. In other words, sanction exists so that a person is not put at a greater disadvantage for obeying the law than the one who violates it. Thus, Hart pointed out that the lack of sanction does not nullify the existence of law (as Austin described) but may reduce its efficacy.

Dhaka, if not the whole of Bangladesh, is facing the same crisis that Hart had warned us about. Due to the limitations in our human nature, there is always a temptation to breach the law for immediate self-interest. However, the social organisations exist so that such violations do not go unpunished. When law imposes sanctions on a particular class of people while others remain unchecked, it not only engenders disparity but also endangers the proper functioning of a society. This also shows why enforcement of law is necessary to a certain extent in order to create a viable social organisation. Because, in the absence of the threat of sanction, breaking the law becomes more profitable than abiding by it. The result is complete chaos, as we now see in Dhaka.

Khalid Khan works as a Law Desk Assistant at Law & Our Rights, The Daily Star.
summary: Dhaka is the noisy, chaotic capital of Bangladesh. Whenever you go out for a walk, you will always find its footpaths occupied by hawkers, often illegally, without having to pay any legal fee.
author: Khalid Khan

title: From Law to Practice: Building Workplaces Free from Sexual Harassment
body:
Bangladesh has taken some important steps towards addressing sexual harassment at work: Sexual harassment is now addressed in the statutory provisions of Bangladesh Labour Act 2006 (the ‘Act’), and ILO Convention No.190 (C190) on Violence and Harassment has also been ratified. With the Bangladesh Labour Rules (the ‘Rules’) now under review, we now have the opportunity to turn these commitments into a system that works in practice. The question is how Bangladesh can create a framework that people in the world of work can trust, organisations can operate, and regulators can enforce.

This is firstly a matter of rights. No one should sacrifice dignity, safety or equality to earn a living. When harassment occurs and no effective response follows, inaction allows the violation of rights to persist. C190 recognises the right to a world of work free from violence and harassment, and calls for prevention, protection, enforcement, remedies and effective investigation.

This is an issue of productivity and organisational-performance as well. In 2018, for example, ILO reported that workplace sexual harassment had cost 2.6 billion dollars in lost productivity, alongside 0.9 billion dollars in other financial costs. Unsafe workplaces can also contribute to absenteeism, turnover, loss of experienced personnel, disengagement and grievances. Poorly handled complaints can turn workplace problems into prolonged disputes, loss of trust, reputational damage and organisational disruption. For organisations, prevention and effective response are therefore not simply compliance costs; they are part of good governance, risk management and institutional performance.

The development sector has an equally important stake. NGOs and development organisations operate within increasingly clear safeguarding and PSEAH expectations from donors, UN agencies and development partners. Policies alone are not enough. Donors need confidence that organisations have safe reporting channels, competent investigations, protection against retaliation, appropriate referral and support mechanisms, and credible systems for responding to concerns. A functioning system protects both people and institutional trust.

For government, this is fundamentally about giving effect to Bangladesh’s international and national commitments. Bangladesh ratified the C190 in November 2025, which will enter into force for Bangladesh on 20 November 2026. C190 calls for an inclusive, integrated and gender-responsive approach to preventing and addressing violence and harassment, including prevention, enforcement, remedies, investigation, training and social dialogue. The current reform of the Rules therefore provides an important opportunity to ensure that Bangladesh’s domestic framework can give practical effect to these commitments.

What needs to happen next?

The next stage should not be to simply add more requirements into the Rules but to ensure that the Act and the Rules operate as one coherent system. To do so, a few measures need to be taken.

First, the relationship between sections 23, 24, 332 and 332A needs to be clarified. Sections 23 and 24 provide the misconduct and disciplinary framework, while sections 332 and 332A address prevention of violence and harassment and establish the complaints committee. The legal framework should clearly explain how an investigation into sexual harassment connects with the disciplinary process when misconduct is established, who initiates disciplinary proceedings, who makes the final decision, and what safeguards apply to all parties.

The objective is not to prejudge a complaint or to make the complaints committee a substitute for disciplinary authority. It is to establish a clear pathway from complaint, investigation and findings to disciplinary decision-making and remedy. If the Act does not provide a sufficient legal basis for that pathway, the relevant provisions of the Act may need amendment. The Rules alone cannot create substantive legal duties or consequences that the Act does not support.

Second, Section 332 needs to be operationalised through the Rules. The amended provision places responsibilities on employers and authorities to prevent violence and harassment and to establish preventive measures. The Rules should translate these broad duties into practical requirements covering workplace policies, risk assessment, awareness and training, reporting, protection and prevention.

Third, Section 332A needs clear procedural and institutional rules. The Act establishes a five-member complaints committee, with a majority of women, a woman chair and two members from organisations working on gender and sexual violence. The committee is expressly responsible for investigating complaints. The Rules should clarify its mandate, competence, independence, timelines, confidentiality, reporting lines and safeguards against interference. They should also clarify how its investigation and findings connect with the formal disciplinary process and the authority responsible for the final decision.

Fourth, the Rules should establish a clear end-to-end process: how a concern is received; how immediate safety is assessed; when a matter proceeds to formal investigation; who investigates; how conflicts of interest are managed; how evidence is assessed; who initiates any disciplinary or other action; who makes the final decision; how the parties are informed; and what remedies and avenues for review are available.

The framework should also recognise that sexual harassment is not always worker-to-worker conduct. It may involve supervisors, managers, contractors, clients, service providers or others connected with the workplace. The system should therefore ensure that a complaint does not fall outside the protection of the framework simply because the complainant or respondent does not fit a narrow statutory category.

Fifth, there must be effective protection against retaliation and victimisation, alongside confidentiality and safe reporting. Protection should extend, where appropriate, to complainants, witnesses, committee members and others participating in a process. At the same time, confidentiality must be balanced with the requirements of a fair investigation and the respondent’s right to know and respond to the relevant allegations.

The system should also distinguish between an unsubstantiated complaint and a deliberately false complaint. Failure to establish an allegation does not, in itself, mean that the complaint was malicious. This distinction is essential to maintaining confidence in reporting while protecting procedural fairness.

Finally, the Rules need to be workable across different sectors and organisational sizes. A multinational, a large factory, an NGO and a smaller enterprise may require different operational arrangements, but all should be capable of meeting the same core principles of prevention, safe reporting, fair investigation, accountability and remedy.

This distinction between Act and Rules matters. The Act should establish the substantive rights, duties, misconduct and protections. The Rules should provide the practical machinery through which those rights and duties can be exercised and enforced. Rules can operationalise the law; they cannot substitute for substantive gaps in the Act.

Why does this matter?

For people in the world of work, a credible system means that speaking up does not risk their livelihood, dignity, safety or professional standing.

For organisations, it provides clarity, consistency and a defensible process for managing workplace risk. It also helps address problems before they become entrenched disputes, turnover, absenteeism or wider disruption.

For workers’ organisations and trade unions, it provides greater confidence that workers can raise concerns and exercise their rights without retaliation. For employers’ organisations and industry associations, a clear and workable framework provides a more level playing field and reduces uncertainty about how cases should be handled.

For government, it demonstrates that Bangladesh’s international commitments are being translated into domestic practice rather than remaining commitments on paper.

For the development sector, credible PSEAH and safeguarding systems are increasingly important to maintaining donor and partner confidence.

For business, the issue extends beyond the workplace itself. Responsible-business expectations increasingly reach into supply chains. Buyers want evidence that labour rights, worker voice, grievance mechanisms, investigation and remedy are functioning in practice, not simply that a policy exists.

There is also a wider market-access dimension. The European Union is Bangladesh’s largest trading partner, and textiles account for the overwhelming majority of EU imports from Bangladesh. Bangladesh currently benefits from the EU’s Everything But Arms (EBA) arrangement. Following LDC graduation, Bangladesh will continue to receive EBA preferences for at least 3 years and has the possibility of seeking GSP+, subject to its conditions. The EU’s revised GSP framework, applying from 1 January 2027, places continued emphasis on human rights, labour rights, sustainable development and good governance.

The supply-chain implications are also becoming more significant. From 14 December 2027, the EU Forced Labour Regulation will prohibit products made with forced labour from being placed on, made available on, or exported from the EU market. True that sexual harassment should not be equated with forced labour. However, violence, intimidation, abuse of vulnerability and other coercive practices can be relevant to wider labour-rights and forced-labour risks. For businesses and supply chains, credible worker voice, grievance, investigation and remedy mechanisms are therefore increasingly being part of responsible risk management.

This matters for Bangladesh’s export-oriented economy. Market access is no longer determined only by price, quality and delivery. Increasingly, buyers, regulators and consumers want confidence that labour rights and responsible-business commitments are implemented in practice. The case is therefore not simply about compliance. It is about good governance and good business.

A credible system can protect rights, reduce avoidable productivity losses, strengthen trust across the workplace, support responsible supply chains, meet Bangladesh’s international commitments, strengthen donor confidence and contribute to continued access to important markets.

These are not competing interests. People in the world of work need protection and remedy. Organisations need clarity and workable processes. Government needs an enforceable framework. Trade unions need confidence in workers’ rights. Development partners need credible safeguarding systems. Industry needs a level playing field. Buyers need confidence in responsible supply chains. They all point towards the same objective: a workplace system that works in practice.

To conclude, a workplace with no complaints may also be a workplace where people do not feel safe enough to speak. Therefore, ‘zero tolerance’ should not mean ‘zero complaints’, but a workplace free from harassment, retaliation and inaction. Bangladesh has moved towards legal reform. The next step is to make the Act and Rules work together in practice. That is where the real test of reform will lie.

The writer is a Barrister-at-Law and Principal of Jenefa Jabbar Consultancy.
summary: Bangladesh has taken some important steps towards addressing sexual harassment at work: Sexual harassment is now addressed in the statutory provisions of Bangladesh Labour Act 2006 (the ‘Act’), and ILO Convention No.190 (C190) on Violence and Harassment has also been ratified.
author: S Sk. Jenefa K. Jabbar

title: Lack of women judges in the Supreme Court
body:
Though hundreds of female judges have been serving in the lower courts across the country with competence and integrity, their presence thins sharply at the Appellate and High Court Divisions of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (SCOB), raising questions over appointments, professional opportunities, and institutional pathways.

While 677 women judges out of total 2,235 are currently serving in the subordinate judiciary, only nine women judges serve in the SCOB. Amongst them, one out of five serves in the Appellate Division and eight out of 99 serve in the High Court Division, sources at the Supreme Court Registrar General’s Office said.

According to some female legal experts, the shortage of female judges is more than a matter of numbers as it reduces the diversity of judicial experience, can weaken women’s confidence in the justice system and creates a visible glass ceiling for women in the legal profession. Meanwhile, Attorney General Md Ruhul Quddus Kazal said that meaningful steps are needed to increase women’s representation in the higher judiciary, while stressing that merit and integrity must remain paramount.

“We should certainly take meaningful steps to increase the representation of women in the judiciary. But while doing so, we must remain extremely cautious to ensure that no unqualified, incompetent, or dishonest person is appointed or elevated merely to achieve gender representation,” he told The Daily Star.

“One of the reasons for the disparity between the representation of men and women in the higher judiciary may be the relatively small number of women lawyers from the Bar who are available for consideration for judicial appointment”, he said.

The attorney general, however noted, “Due to various practical realities, some women lawyers may not be able to remain equally serious or committed to the profession over the long term. At the same time, perhaps we have not done enough to make the legal profession more attractive and supportive for women or to retain them in the profession”.

“I can see a practical example of this myself in the case of appointments to the Attorney General's Office. We have around 270 Law Officers, but only a handful—perhaps 10 to 12—are women lawyers. There is comparatively less interest among women lawyers in joining this office. One possible reason is that, in the professional environment, they may not always have sufficient opportunities to demonstrate their professional abilities and make their mark on an equal footing with their male counterparts”.

“Therefore, in my view, we should focus on developing the skills and capabilities of women lawyers and, at the same time, create a professional environment in which they can remain in the legal profession for the long term and have adequate opportunities to demonstrate their abilities. In this way, we should seek to reduce, as far as possible, the disparity between the representation of men and women in the higher judiciary”, the attorney general further added.

Barrister Ruhul Quddus Kazal also said that anyone appointed to any position must meet the standards of both competence and integrity. “A person should not be appointed to any position, particularly in the higher judiciary, merely on the basis of being a woman or a man if that person is otherwise unqualified, incompetent, or lacking in integrity”, he cautioned.

“Very recently, we have witnessed the resignation or retirement of several judges of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. Some of them were unable to continue performing their judicial duties until the end of their judicial careers. In some cases, their service came to an end after prolonged periods of leave. It has also been reported that there are specific allegations of corruption against some female judges in similar circumstances,” he added.

Barrister Sarwat Siraj Shukla, a senior Supreme Court lawyer, told this correspondent that it is unfortunate that Bangladesh is yet to get its first female chief justice.

“The number of female judges in High Court Division is negligible. Only a handful of women have made it to the Appellate Division. There are significant number of competent female judges in our subordinate courts. However, they do not find their way into our higher judiciary. There is scope to increase the intake from subordinate to judiciary”.

“Scarcity of competent senior female lawyers in our higher judiciary is one of the reasons why we do not have sufficient intake from the bar. It will take time to create an ecosystem conducive to preparing women lawyers fit to be judges. It is high time a temporary measure is taken by the government to ensure that certain percentage of judges are women,” she added.

Advocate Ishrat Hasan told this newspaper that the fact that 677 women serve in the subordinate judiciary while only nine serve in the Appellate and High Court Divisions shows that the problem is not a lack of qualified women but limited institutional pathways to the higher judiciary.

“Unlike recruitment to the judicial service through competitive examinations, appointments to the Supreme Court under Article 95 of the Constitution lack sufficiently transparent, measurable and gender-responsive criteria. The limited elevation of experienced female District and Sessions Judges, unequal family responsibilities and restricted access to professional networks further widen this gap”, she said.

The lawyer added that although judicial decisions must be based on law and evidence rather than gender, the shortage of women judges reduces diversity of judicial experience, weakens women’s confidence in the justice system and creates a visible glass ceiling for female judges and lawyers.

“In light of Articles 27 and 28 of the Constitution, Bangladesh should adopt a transparent judicial appointment law, ensure the meaningful inclusion of qualified women in shortlists, elevate more experienced women from the subordinate judiciary and publish gender-disaggregated appointment data. This is not a concession to women or a compromise on merit; it is necessary for substantive equality, public confidence and a stronger, more representative judiciary,” she added further.

Advocate Tasmiah Nuhiya Ahmed, another Supreme Court lawyer, said, “the significant gap between women’s representation in Bangladesh’s subordinate judiciary and the Supreme Court deserves serious institutional attention. The presence of hundreds of female judges in the lower judiciary proves that Bangladesh has no shortage of qualified, capable and experienced women judges. Yet, their numbers decline sharply at the higher level.”

She said that the issue is not competence or availability, but the pathway to appointment and elevation to the SC.

“Unlike the comparatively structured judicial service system, SC appointments follow a different constitutional process. Historically, women have been underrepresented among both senior lawyers and judges elevated from the subordinate judiciary, narrowing the pipeline to the highest level,” she said.

The lawyer added that greater gender diversity can strengthen public confidence and bring broader professional and life experiences to the judiciary, particularly in cases involving women and children. She stressed that appointments should never be based on quotas or compromise merit. Instead, equally qualified women should receive fair consideration, including experienced female judges and distinguished women lawyers.

“A more transparent and structured appointment process, balancing merit, integrity, professional excellence and diversity, could help ensure that women’s progress in the lower judiciary is reflected at the SC level”, Tasmiah opined.

Ashutosh Sarkar is a senior reporter at the Daily Star.
summary: Though hundreds of female judges have been serving in the lower courts across the country with competence and integrity, their presence thins sharply at the Appellate and High Court Divisions of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (SCOB), raising questions over appointments, professional opportunities, and institutional pathways.
author: Ashutosh Sarkar

title: The proposed Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act and free speech
body:
The Cyber Protection Act, 2026 (the ‘Act’) is the primary law regulating Bangladeshi citizens’ activities online. Recently, an Amendment bill has been proposed, and it has garnered the attention of netizens for some of its vague provisions.

Firstly, the proposed amendment introduces section 26A, which criminalises sharing ‘unverified information’ (not false information) online with up to 10 years of imprisonment. Due to the ambiguous nature of the term, it may be interpreted as any information pending confirmation by the government, thereby broadening the ambit of police powers. As a result, it may impede the ordinary functions of a free press, e.g., journalism, eyewitness reporting, and citizen accounts of a death during a protest, published before an official statement arrives.

Next, section 25 currently covers sexual harassment, blackmail, revenge pornography, and child sexual abuse material. However, the proposed amendment quietly folds ‘defamation’ and ‘humiliation’ into that same list and doubles the penalties across the board: from 2 years of imprisonment to 5 years in general, and from 5 years of imprisonment to 10 years for offences against women. The vagueness in the newly added definitions is, arguably, a deliberate choice, not a lapse in drafting skill.

On the other hand, section 8 currently allows only law enforcement agencies to seek the blocking of online content for narrowly listed reasons. However, under the proposed amendment, the Ministry of Information, along with other unnamed empowered agencies, is also granted the same powers. Moreover, the requirement of obtaining judicial approval after blocking or removing content is also done away with. Rather, the proposed amended section requires the aggrieved person to apply before the agency or the court to make the removed or blocked content accessible again. Meaning, in practice, the same body imposing a block will also become the adjudicating forum for its own cause, violating the cardinal principle of natural justice - ‘No one should be the judge of their own case.’

The incoherence of the maximum penalties prescribed in the new draft is also noticeable. The draft amendment prescribes ten years of punishment for both cyber-terrorism causing death or serious injury and the offence of sharing fake news online. This cannot be explained by any theory of proportionate punishment. A law that punishes the ‘offence’ of sharing unverified information as severely as an act of terrorism cannot be deemed to be concerned about preventing harm but about preventing speech.

Unfortunately, Bangladesh has run this experiment before. The Digital Security Act of 2018 produced over a thousand cases and arrests in five years, disproportionately targeting politicians and journalists. Notably, the writer Mushtaq Ahmed died in prison, and Ahmed Kishore was arrested for drawing cartoons under that repressive law. Renamed as the Cyber Security Act in 2023, the law kept nearly all of its repressive provisions intact, according to Amnesty International's own review. It took Bangladesh years and a change of government to undo that structure and enact a better law. Unfortunately, this amendment is once again taking us backwards.

To conclude, a cyber security law which curtails freedom of expression disproportionately fails its stated purpose. The remedy for wrong information has always been better information, not imprisonment. I believe the Parliament should withdraw the amendment and let the current Act remain intact.

The writer is a civil and political activist and a researcher at Human Rights Support Society.
summary: The Cyber Protection Act, 2026 (the ‘Act’) is the primary law regulating Bangladeshi citizens’ activities online. Recently, an Amendment bill has been proposed, and it has garnered the attention of netizens for some of its vague provisions.
author: A Abdullah Al Bukhari

title: The worker at the end of the supply chain
body:
Globalization has a habit of making people disappear.

We see the container ship, but not the hands that packed the box. We see the global brand, but rarely the worker who stitched the shirt. We celebrate exports, foreign investment and integration into world markets, while the human being at the far end of the supply chain is often reduced to a statistic.

Abdullah Al Faruque’s Globalization and Labour Rights: Lessons from the Experiences of Bangladesh attempts to reverse this disappearance. The book begins with a deceptively simple premise: globalization is not merely an economic phenomenon. It is also a story about power, law and work. As capital, technology and production cross borders, the boundaries of the workplace and the nation-state become increasingly porous. For workers, this can mean opportunity and insecurity at the same time-new jobs alongside precarious employment, and greater participation in the global economy alongside diminished bargaining power.

For Bangladesh, few questions are more consequential. Over several decades, Bangladesh has moved deeply into the global economy through trade liberalisation, foreign investment and export-oriented production. This transformation has generated employment and increased women’s participation in paid work. Yet it has also brought informalisation, insecure employment and new forms of vulnerability. Dr. Faruque wisely avoids presenting globalization as either salvation or catastrophe. Its consequences, he argues, depend substantially on the institutions that govern it.

That refusal to offer an easy verdict is one of the book’s principal virtues.
