Across 12 chapters, the author examines industrial relations, labour-law institutions, export processing zones, trade unions, collective bargaining, minimum wages, dispute settlement, international labour standards, social dialogue, post-Rana Plaza initiatives and migrant workers. The subjects are diverse, but they converge on one question: how can workers exercise meaningful rights when the economic forces shaping their working lives increasingly operate beyond national borders?

Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry provides the clearest window into this dilemma. The sector has become one of the country’s defining links with the global economy, creating employment on a vast scale and transforming the lives of millions, particularly women. But its success has also exposed the fault lines of global production: low wages, long hours, unsafe workplaces and restrictions on labour rights. The garments sold in affluent markets may travel thousands of miles from factories where workers have little influence over the price, timetable or conditions of production.

Dr. Faruque’s discussion of global supply chains is especially revealing because it exposes the geography of value. Bangladesh largely occupies the lower-value stages of production-cutting, making, trimming and shipping-while design, branding, logistics and retail intelligence tend to sit elsewhere. The supply chain is therefore global not only in distance but also in power.

This is where the book moves beyond conventional labour-law analysis. The traditional model-state, employer, worker and union operating within a national framework-has been unsettled by multinational corporations, international buyers, private compliance schemes, transnational unions and multi-stakeholder organisations. Labour governance is no longer confined neatly within national borders.

The Rana Plaza disaster remains the darkest symbol of this transformation. In 2013, the collapse of Rana Plaza killed more than 1,000 workers and forced the world to confront the human foundations of an industry whose products were sold far beyond Bangladesh. In its aftermath came initiatives including the Accord and the Alliance, alongside wider efforts to improve factory safety and supply-chain governance. Dr. Faruque examines these developments as experiments in transnational and private regulation, raising a larger question: who should bear responsibility for labour conditions when a supply chain stretches across continents?

Yet the book does not confine the labour question to the garment factory. One of its important insights is that the most vulnerable worker may be the one who never enters the formal workplace. Informal employment dominates Bangladesh’s labour market, according to the figures cited in the book, leaving a huge proportion of workers outside the effective reach of formal employment protections. Such workers may lack secure wages, fixed hours, paid leave, occupational safety and meaningful representation.

The emerging gig economy adds another layer of uncertainty. Digital platforms, freelancing, ride-sharing and delivery services may offer flexibility, but they raise familiar questions in new forms: Who is the employer? Who bears responsibility for social security? What constitutes a fair wage when the worker is technically independent? The technology may be new; the struggle over power and protection is not.

Trade unions consequently occupy an uneasy place in this landscape. Globalisation can weaken unions by fragmenting production and employment, encouraging subcontracting and eroding the standard employment relationship. Yet it can also create possibilities for transnational worker solidarity. If capital can organise across borders, labour may increasingly need to learn to do the same.

The discussion of international labour standards adds another layer. Bangladesh has ratified most of the ILO’s core conventions, and many international principles have found recognition in domestic law. Yet the distance between legal recognition and everyday enforcement remains substantial. Informality, weak enforcement, inadequate resources and precarious employment complicate the translation of rights from paper into practice.

Dr. Faruque’s treatment of human rights due diligence gives the book a particularly contemporary edge. Developments in the UK, France, Australia and Germany, as well as the European Union, increasingly require companies to identify, prevent and address human-rights risks in their supply chains. For Bangladeshi exporters, compliance is therefore becoming more than a voluntary exercise in corporate responsibility; it is increasingly part of a wider regulatory expectation.

The book’s breadth is both its strength and, occasionally, its limitation. Its wide-ranging treatment means that some subjects receive more conceptual than empirical attention. Yet that breadth is also what makes the work valuable. Labour law does not exist in a vacuum. Workers’ rights are shaped by trade policy, corporate structures, migration regimes, technology, union strength and the ability of public institutions to enforce the law.

Ultimately, Globalization and Labour Rights is less a verdict on globalization than an invitation to see it differently. The book reminds us that markets do not write labour law; institutions do. Globalization may create jobs and opportunities, but without effective institutions it can also distribute its risks disproportionately to those least able to bear them.

The irony is that the more interconnected the world becomes, the easier it can be to forget the individual worker within the machinery of connection. Dr. Faruque’s achievement is to put that worker back into the picture.

In the end, the book asks a question that reaches far beyond Bangladesh: when the world’s economy becomes global, can justice remain local? Its answer is not simple. But its warning is clear: unless rights travel as far as capital does, the promise of globalization will remain incomplete.
summary: Globalization has a habit of making people disappear.
author: Fowzul Azim

title: Bangladesh’s measles crisis and the question of legal responsibility
body:
Measles is amongst the most preventable diseases known to medicine. A single vaccine, dosed twice, prevents it in the overwhelming majority of children. So, when nearly a thousand children have died of measles in a nationwide outbreak since March this year, coinciding with the steepest decline in Bangladesh’s vaccine coverage, from nearly 99.7 per cent as recently as in 2021 to roughly 56–59 per cent by 2025, well below the 95 per cent threshold needed to interrupt transmission, one must ask: was this risk foreseeable, and if so, did the state do enough to avert it?

In fact, in early September, the High Court Division (HCD) of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (SCOB) has issued a rule asking why the family of a measles victim should not receive Tk 1 crore in compensation.

Constitutionally speaking, Article 15(a) imposes securing medical care among the fundamental responsibilities of the State, while Article 18(1) places public health among the State’s primary duties. However, both of these provisions are part of the fundamental principles of state policy, and thus, according to Article 8(2), are judicially unenforceable. Meaning, although the Constitution recognises the importance of public health, it does not, systematically, allow a citizen to demand vaccination as an enforceable constitutional right. The workaround can be found through Article 32’s protection of life, which has long been interpreted by our courts as a concept beyond mere physical existence, including protection against foreseeable and preventable threats to survival.

Moreover, the Infectious Diseases (Prevention, Control and Elimination) Act 2018 is the primary legislation that governs issues relating to prevention and control of such diseases in Bangladesh. Section 4 provides a list of infectious diseases, which is non-exhaustive, and the Government may, by gazette, bring any emerging or re-emerging diseases within the Act. The Act further places broad preventive responsibilities on the health authorities in its provisions, including duties to inspect and monitor suspected infections, declare an infected area, and take necessary measures to contain and prevent the transmission. Further, sections 25 and 26 provide for penal sanctions against individuals concealing an infection or disregarding any administrative orders directed under the Act. However, the Act does not prescribe a mandatory minimum vaccine reserve, impose a legal obligation to report a stockout, or establish a minimum coverage threshold. Section 32 empowers the government to make rules, but the Act nowhere specifies how the state should manage an emergency outbreak like the present one.

So when the state outright cancelled a previously deferred supplementary immunisation campaign rather than rescheduling it, or when it moved away from UNICEF’s vaccination procurement channel toward a competitive-tender-based system, despite explicit and repeated warnings of the risks, followed by a severe decline in vaccination coverage and ultimately, the outbreak - none of it, strictly speaking, breached a legal duty. This is because the statute only contemplates the citizens failing the state, not the other way around.

India shows that the alternative is not necessarily hypothetical. Its Epidemic Diseases Act 1897, together with the Disaster Management Act 2005, gives the State explicit emergency powers over public health, and a number of significant case precedents have been set out in this regard. The 2021 case of In Re: Distribution of Essential Supplies and Services During Pandemic (2021), where the Indian Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance of the second COVID-19 wave; or the 2026 case, Rachana Gangu v Union of India, where the court ordered a no-fault compensation framework, holding that grave harm following a state-led public health intervention imposes a positive obligation on the state, can be exemplary for Bangladesh.

International law establishes a general preventive standard. Article 12 of ICESCR requires the States to take measures for the prevention, treatment and control of epidemics and other diseases. Similarly, Article 24 of the UNCRC mandates the States to pursue appropriate measures to ensure the highest attainable right to health for children.

In conclusion, the 2018 Act should be amended to require a minimum and publicly disclosed vaccine reserve, a scientific coverage threshold and a no-fault compensation framework. Ultimately, the aim is not to make the State responsible for every outbreak that occurs, but to establish a legally responsible framework that will ensure a timely response, so when a similar crisis emerges, the State speaks with action rather than regret.

Irna Jahan Shejuti is a student of law, University of Dhaka.
summary: Measles is amongst the most preventable diseases known to medicine.
author: I Irna Jahan Shejuti

title: How to ensure responsible use of AI in the courtroom
body:
Should artificial intelligence (AI) be allowed inside the courtroom, and if so, how far should its role extend? The question has moved at an alarming speed from academic seminars to daily practice. The most contentious issue is judgment writing itself, where the spectre of AI “hallucination”, confident, plausible-sounding, entirely fabricated output, has already embarrassed courts in several jurisdictions. What was once a theoretical concern for lawyers and academics has now become a question of judicial governance.

Research increasingly shows how deeply AI has entered judicial systems. A Northwestern University study published in March 2026, based on a stratified random survey of active US federal judges, found that more than 60 per cent of respondents had used at least one AI tool in their judicial work, though mostly for legal research and document review, not for drafting judgments. This distinction matters because when properly deployed, AI can certainly assist in converting voluminous and disorganised case records into neutral, structured summaries, highlighting relevant issues, evidence, chronology, and inconsistencies without interfering with judicial reasoning. However, when used without adequate safeguards, it may undermine independent verification by encouraging reliance on algorithmic outputs that may appear authoritative despite being erroneous.

In Bangladesh, AI tools are already in use in courtrooms and chambers across the country, but there is no practice direction governing when, how, or by whom they may be used. According to the Law Minister’s statement in Parliament this year, nearly 4.64 million cases remained pending across all levels of the judiciary as of March 31, 2026, the overwhelming majority stuck in the lower courts. Efficient and cautious use of AI could organise records, speed up research, cut the time spent on routine administrative work, and free up judges for the actual work of adjudication.

However, the drawbacks of using AI are also significant. By now, the story of lawyers citing fictitious, AI-generated judgments is a common phenomenon. A database named Damien Charlotin has logged over 2,000 such incidents worldwide as of this month, most from the United States but a growing number elsewhere, including India. In one case recorded there, the Supreme Court of India set aside a customs authority’s order and remanded it for fresh consideration after finding that the decision appeared to rely on judgments and commentary generated by AI, some of which simply did not exist.

Some jurisdictions have decided to write rules on the use of AI. The EU’s AI Act sorts systems into four risk tiers and bans the “unacceptable” tier outright. Similarly, in June 2026, the AI committee of the Supreme Court of India published draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026, built on five principles: human primacy, transparency, accountability, data protection, and judicial independence. The draft says that AI may assist with judicial work but never perform it itself. For instance, it cannot decide bail eligibility, assess witness credibility, predict recidivism or flight risk, etc. And crucially, no officer can cite a tool’s hallucination as an excuse for a wrong decision; the human stays accountable, always.

Bangladesh, on the other hand, still has no dedicated framework for AI in its courts. The draft National AI Policy 2024 gestures toward the judiciary as a “high-risk” domain but stops there; it doesn’t spell out enforceable rules for judges, lawyers, or court staff. That gap needs closing soon, before informal, unmonitored use hardens into unaccountable habit.

What would a workable framework actually look like? We would like to propose that a workable framework should contain, at the very least, the following three elements. First, a clear and public list of what is permitted and what is not. Legal research, case-record summarisation, translation, transcription, hearing scheduling, and case management could all sit on the permitted side. Second, where AI use has materially contributed to a filing, lawyers and litigants should be required to disclose it. — and that use should be subject to verification by the lawyer and the presiding judge alike, not left to trust. Third and finally, an AI committee under the supervision of the Supreme Court could identify permissible and prohibited uses, issue practice directions for judges and advocates, certify AI tools, conduct regular technical and ethical audits, and supervise complaints arising from the district courts.

Two further safeguards should be incorporated alongside these. Data protection needs to be built in from the start. AI systems should have access only to what a given task actually requires, and judgments or other judicial material used to train or fine-tune such systems should be properly anonymised first. And judges, court staff and lawyers need basic AI-literacy training, not to instil blind trust in the technology, nor blanket suspicion of it, but informed, responsible use. In fact, none of this needs to wait for new legislation. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh can issue such practice directions on its own authority.

In conclusion, responsible use of AI for research, drafting, and administrative work could genuinely help raise disposal rates and ease the backlog if it is allowed to. But without adequate safeguards, it can just as easily become a new source of error in a system that can least afford.

Arzin Nawar is a student of BRAC University, Dr Tahura is a judge, Nusiba Hasan Ohee is a student of Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP).
summary: Should artificial intelligence (AI) be allowed inside the courtroom, and if so, how far should its role extend?
author: D Dr. Ummey Sharaban Tahura N Nusiba Hasan Ohee A Arzin Nawar

title: A new start for Bangladesh's National Human Rights Commission: The Real Test Begins Now
body:
On 6 September, Parliament adopted a new legal framework for Bangladesh's National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), an institution that has long faced criticism over its independence and effectiveness. The new framework introduces useful measures that we firmly welcome, including a simpler complaints process, interim orders to protect people facing immediate harm, the requirement that Commissioners work full time, and a National Preventive Mechanism unit to help prevent torture and ill-treatment in places of detention.

The Principles relating to the Status of National Institutions for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights (the Paris Principles), adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1993, provide the relevant international benchmark: national human rights institutions should be independent and pluralistic, possess a broad mandate and have sufficient powers and resources to carry out that mandate. The new framework should now be implemented in accordance with these principles. While legislation can create the conditions for progress, public confidence depends on how things work in practice.

The NHRC’s ultimate measure of success will be its effectiveness in protecting human rights and ensuring access to remedies for victims. This is why, throughout the process of drafting the new law, we encouraged efforts to ensure a transparent and merit-based process of appointing a capable and independent NHRC leadership, including men and women and representatives of minorities reflecting Bangladesh’s diverse society. Bangladesh can certainly draw on an impressive array of individuals with a track record of integrity and courage, who may lead the NHRC and ensure the definitive break with the past that we recognise underpins the law. We hope it does so. Such individuals will, no doubt, be needed to help address difficult and politically sensitive issues, ensure the NHRC exercises its mandate without fear or favour, and hold disciplined and security forces and other public institutions accountable.

The National Preventive Mechanism is particularly significant. We welcomed Bangladesh's accession to the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture (OPCAT) in 2025. As we move forward with implementation, regular unannounced visits to places of detention will be important for prevention and meeting the commitments undertaken through OPCAT. Operational independence, specialist personnel, adequate resources and unhindered access to sites of detention and to detainees are, we know from experience, part and parcel of an effective NPM, which in turn strengthens public institutions.

A further issue of central importance is that any national human rights institution must be able to respond wherever serious violations are alleged, irrespective of the institution concerned. The effectiveness of the NHRC will depend on how it uses its powers to promote prompt, impartial and thorough investigations, protect complainants and victims, and publish clear recommendations. The authorities, in turn, should respond fully and transparently. If experience shows that legal restrictions prevent effective oversight or remedy, there may be a case for Parliament to revisit those provisions.

The Commission cannot succeed alone. The Government and Parliament must safeguard its independence and respond to its findings. We encourage the establishment of a new culture of cooperation between the NHRC and the judiciary, law-enforcement and security institutions, civil society, human rights defenders, the legal profession and the media. The Commission’s credibility will also rest on its ability to communicate clearly, publish its findings and demonstrate that every complaint is treated with seriousness and impartiality. International partners will now follow the implementation of the law closely and share technical expertise and international good practice to support an effective and independent NHRC.

Carol Flore-Smereczniak, Resident Coordinator a.i. United Nations in Bangladesh

Michael Miller, Ambassador & Head of Delegation of the European Union to Bangladesh

Sarah Cooke, British High Commissioner to Bangladesh

Ajit Singh, High Commissioner of Canada to Bangladesh

Christian Brix Møller, Ambassador of Denmark to Bangladesh

Joris van Bommel, Ambassador of the Netherlands to Bangladesh

Håkon Arald Gulbrandsen, Ambassador of Norway to Bangladesh

Stephen Rodriques, Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Programme in Bangladesh.
summary: On 6 September, Parliament adopted a new legal framework for Bangladesh's National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), an institution that has long faced criticism over its independence and effectiveness.

body:
Unidentified criminals shot a local Jubo Dal leader and a grocery shop owner in separate incidents in Khulna yesterday.

In Terokhada upazila, Ramim Biswas, 32, president of Jubo Dal’s ward-3 unit in Madhupur union, suffered a bullet wound in an attack by armed assailants in Parhaji village around 11:10am, said Kabir Hossain, inspector (investigation) of Terokhada Police Station.

According to a press release issued by district police, Ramim was sitting in a van in front of a house near Khan Bricks in Parhaji village, along the Sen-er Bazar-Madhupur Road. At that time, unidentified assailants on a motorcycle fired at him from behind and fled the scene. A bullet hit his rib cage.

Meanwhile, in the district town, grocery shop owner Dhananjay Kundu, alias Akash Kundu, 45, of the Gachhtala Temple area, was shot on Dakshin Tutpara Cross Road around 6:45pm, said Khulna Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge of Lokmon Hossain.

Quoting witnesses, the OC said the assailants arrived on a motorcycle, fired a single shot at Akash and fled the scene. Akash sustained a gunshot wound to his abdomen.

Both of them were rescued by locals and taken to Khulna Medical College Hospital.

The identities of the attackers and the motive behind the shootings were not immediately known, police said.

Security was beefed up following the shooting.

The incidents took place on the same day the inspector general of police was on an official visit in the district. IGP Ali Hossain Fakir visited Khulna Police Lines and met police personnel and representatives of different policing committees.

The shootings come amid growing concerns over law and order in Khulna.

According to district police data, 35 murders were reported in Khulna district between January and the first week of October this year. Police had solved 25 of the cases, while the remaining 10 were yet to be solved, Khulna Superintendent of Police Sarker Omar Faroque said earlier.

Meanwhile, Khulna Metropolitan Police (KMP) recorded 33 murders in the city between January and September. Police claimed to have solved 31 of the cases.

According to a police list, at least 10 major criminal gangs are active in Khulna city. Clashes, retaliatory attacks, and killings have occurred among these groups over territorial control and revenge.

A joint force has launched a special operation in four upazilas to improve law and order, with a focus on curbing drug-related crimes and recovering illegal firearms.

The operation began on October 6 in Rupsha, Dighalia, Terokhada, and Batiaghata upazilas, involving the Special Response Battalion (formerly RAB), KMP, and district police.

“Most of the targeted killings in Khulna are linked to drug-related activities,” the SP told The Daily Star.

A 40-year-old woman was allegedly tortured and had her hair chopped off by a group of locals in Jhenaidah Sadar upazila.

The incident took place on Thursday afternoon. The victim filed a case against five people with Jhenaidah Sadar Police Station that night, police said today.

Speaking to The Daily Star, the woman said she was sitting at home on Thursday afternoon while her son was sleeping in another room. At that time, a man named Abdur Rashid from a neighbouring village went to her house and accused her of having an extramarital relationship with one Anwar Hossain.

Shortly afterwards, Anwar’s wife, two daughters and a son entered the house. They allegedly grabbed the woman by her hair, forced her to the ground, cut her hair and smeared chilli powder on parts of her body.

Hearing her screams, the woman’s son woke up and came to intervene, but he was also beaten up, the victim said.

The woman later received treatment from a local village doctor.

She said she filed a written complaint with Jhenaidah Sadar Police Station that night.

The woman’s son told The Daily Star that, “When I tried to stop them, they beat me too. Abdur Rashid, a local influential person, was present and took part in torturing my mother and me,” he said.

Locals alleged that Rashid identifies himself as a political leader.

When this correspondent visited Rashid’s home to seek his response to the allegations, he was not found. His mobile phone was switched off.

Sheikh Billal Hossain, additional superintendent of police (finance and administration) in Jhenaidah, told The Daily Star that the victim had filed a case naming five people: Anwar Hossain’s wife, two daughters and son, and Abdur Rashid.

According to the police official, the woman stated in her complaint that members of Anwar’s family had allegedly tortured her in a similar incident about a year and a half ago.

Police are conducting raids to arrest the accused, the additional SP added.

Cumilla police have submitted a chargesheet in the murder case of 13-year-old Ishiat Shahriar Oprotim, accusing four people, including two juveniles.

The chargesheet was submitted on October 20, Lutfor Rahman, additional superintendent of police, told The Daily Star yesterday.

According to the chargesheet, Oprotim was killed after resisting an attempt to snatch his iPhone. He was allegedly struck on the head with the handle of a spade during the attack.

The incident occurred on September 18 between 5:00pm and 6:00pm in the Sananda area of Lalmai Hill.

The accused are Saiful Islam Tuhin, Md Siam, and two 15-year-olds. Police said all four were involved in planning the crime, while Tuhin and the two 15-year-olds directly participated in the killing.

KM Firoz Shahriar, the victim’s father, said, “The investigating officer called around 12:30am [yesterday] to inform that the chargesheet had been submitted to the court.”

Demanding a speedy trial, he said he hoped the court would hand down the maximum punishment to those responsible and that the accused should not escape accountability because of their age.

According to jail authorities, Tuhin and Siam are in Cumilla Central Jail, while the two teenagers are currently being held at the juvenile development centre in Gazipur.

A madrasa teacher was detained last night over allegations of sexually harassing a student at a residential girls’ madrasa in Pabna Sadar upazila. Enraged locals later vandalised the institution and set it on fire early today.

The incident took place at Nurani Madrasa in Dorivaudanga village under Varara union of Pabna Sadar upazila.

According to police and locals, the arrested teacher, Md Abu Eusuf Pramanik of Khalishpur village, had been teaching at the madrasa for the past five years.

Inspector (Investigation) Sanjoy Kumar Shaha said the accused allegedly attempted to molest a student last night; the student managed to escape and informed locals.

An angry crowd then rushed to the madrasa, caught the teacher and beat him severely, prompting police to arrive at the scene, rescue him and take him into custody, the inspector said.

The madrasa has 60 students, including 30 residential students. Following the incident, outraged locals gathered to protest the alleged misconduct.

Police subsequently rescued the residential students and handed them over to their parents later that night.

However, angry locals vandalised the madrasa building and set it on fire early Friday morning.

“We are working to take legal action against the accused teacher,” Inspector Shaha said.

Police said preparations were under way to file a case over the incident.

The situation in the area remained tense, with additional police forces deployed to maintain order.

Police have submitted a chargesheet in the murder case of 13-year-old Ishiat Shahriar Oprotim, naming four people, including two juveniles, as accused in the killing.

The chargesheet was submitted on October 20 by the case's investigating officer, Rajib Ahmed, Additional Superintendent of Police Lutfor Rahman confirmed to The Daily Star today.

According to the chargesheet, Oprotim was killed after resisting an attempt to snatch his iPhone. He was allegedly struck on the head with the handle of a spade during the attack.

The accused are Saiful Islam Tuhin, Md Siam, and two 15-year-olds. Police said all four were involved in planning the crime, while Tuhin and the two 15-year-olds directly participated in the killing.

KM Firoz Shahriar, the victim's father and the plaintiff in the case, said, "The investigating officer called around 12:30am to inform that the chargesheet had been submitted to the court." He added that he would meet the investigating officer today.Demanding a speedy trial, he said he hoped the court would hand down the maximum punishment to those responsible and that the accused should not escape accountability because of their age.

A madrasa teacher was sent to jail on Thursday in a case filed against him for allegedly sexually harassing a seven-year-old female student of the institution.

The accused, Moslem Ahmed, 30, is the vice-principal of the madrasa in Tongi, Gazipur.

On Wednesday, the girl’s relatives and local residents beat up Moslem and handed him over to police.

He was subsequently arrested in a case filed by the girl’s father under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act and produced before a court on Thursday. The judge ordered that he be sent to jail, said Tongi West Police Station Officer-in-Charge Arifur Rahman.

According to the girl’s family, Moslem sexually harassed the first-grader on the madrasa’s ground-floor staircase on October 20 and threatened to beat her if she told anyone.

Frightened, the girl stopped attending the madrasa for three consecutive days. When her family asked her why, she told her parents about the incident.

After learning about it, her father went to the madrasa on Wednesday afternoon and sought an explanation from the vice-principal.

As news spread, agitated local residents gathered on the premises, surrounded Moslem and beat him up.

On information, Tongi West police rushed to the scene, rescued him and took him into custody.

Meanwhile, the madrasa authorities filed a separate complaint with police alleging vandalism and assaults on teachers.

Several videos showing Moslem being beaten have been circulating on Facebook since Thursday.

In a 24-second video, several people are seen questioning Moslem. He is heard saying that he has a “different kind of relationship” with students, particularly first-graders. When he mentions kissing, several of the girl’s relatives slap and beat him.

Another clip, lasting two minutes and 29 seconds, shows several people beating the teacher while others try to stop them.

The girl’s relatives alleged that the madrasa authorities had taken no action despite being informed about the incident.

However, Almas Hossain, founder and principal of the madrasa, claimed that the incident had been orchestrated by a group of 15-16 people to damage the institution’s reputation.

He alleged that other teachers and security personnel were also assaulted while trying to save Moslem. He further claimed that the madrasa office was vandalised and Tk 17 lakh and five mobile phones were looted.

The girl’s father denied the allegation of looting.

He also said he had been receiving death threats from various quarters since the incident, with threatening comments being posted about him on social media, leaving him feeling unsafe.

OC Arifur said police would investigate the matter and take further action as necessary.

Allegations of rape, attempted rape, and sexual abuse of children at six madrasas in just 16 days have sparked public outrage.

There have been protests, assaults on accused teachers, vandalism, and arson.

The incidents, reported between October 8 and 23 in Gazipur, Dhaka’s Savar, Kushtia and Pabna, involved boys and girls as young as seven. Several were allegedly threatened into silence.

Rights groups have raised concerns over madrasa students’ safety, warning that protests alone cannot ensure their protection. They called for stronger and coordinated monitoring and anti-sexual harassment panels at every institution.

The incidents are disturbing.

In Gazipur’s Gacha, teacher Md Oliullah Islam, 23, allegedly raped an eight-year-old residential student at Darul Hedayah Qawmi Madrasa on three consecutive nights (October 10, 11 and 12) and threatened him into silence.

The boy told his mother on October 13, prompting her to file a case. Police arrested Oliullah and governing body member Mohammad Mizan, 38, on October 22. Both were sent to jail the next day, while another accused, Md Abdul Quddus Sheikh, 45, remains at large.

In Tongi, Moslem Ahmed, 30, teacher of Qariul Quran International Madrasa, allegedly sexually abused a seven-year-old Class-I girl on October 19, her family said.

Threatened with a beating if she spoke out, the girl stayed away from classes for three days before telling her parents.

Relatives and locals assaulted Moslem on October 21 before police rescued and detained him. The girl’s father filed a case on October 22, when a court sent Moslem to jail.

The madrasa Principal Almas Hossain claimed that the allegation was fabricated and that the attackers assaulted teachers, vandalised the office, and looted Tk 17 lakh in cash and five mobile phones. The girl’s father denied the looting allegation. Madrasa authorities filed a separate case on October 23.

In Savar, madrasa owner and headteacher Abdul Bari, 50, allegedly raped a 13-year-old residential student on October 21 and threatened to kill her if she spoke out.

His wife, Tohfa, 40, was detained that evening and arrested following a case filed on October 22 accusing her of aiding the rape and threatening the girl. Bari remains at large.

Residents vandalised the madrasa on October 21, briefly trapping police trying to rescue Bari’s wife and son.

Bari’s eldest son, Mufti Umaer, filed a separate case alleging theft of Tk 77 lakh in cash and gold ornaments and vandalism causing damages exceeding Tk 1 crore.

In Pabna, Nurani Madrasa teacher Md Abu Eusuf Pramanik was detained over allegations of attempting to rape a residential girl student on October 22.

The girl escaped and alerted locals, who assaulted him before handing him over to police. He was jailed after her family filed a case.

Residents vandalised and torched the madrasa early on October 23.

In Kushtia’s Daulatpur, Darul Abbar Madrasa teacher Sayeed Hossain Nannu allegedly attempted to rape a Class-III girl on October 14 but fled when her screams alerted locals.

Her mother filed a complaint on October 20. Police arrested him, and a court sent him to jail on October 21.

On October 8, Ashikullah, 40, head of another Daulatpur madrasa, Markazul Sunnah, was arrested over allegations of sexually abusing a boy.

Thousands surrounded the madrasa, and several police personnel were injured trying to rescue him.

Police said Ashikullah was sent to jail.

Asked about the incidents in madrasas, Religious Affairs Minister Kazi Shah Mofazzal Hossain Kaikobad yesterday said the alleged abuse was “extremely distressing and shameful” and pledged preventive measures.

“We’ll do whatever is necessary in this regard...,” he told journalists after attending the triennial council session of the Bangladesh National Imam Association in Agargaon.

He said he had urged imams to explain permissible and forbidden conduct under Islamic teachings during Friday sermons.

The prime minister was also aware and had issued instructions to prevent such abuse, he added.

Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh, a Qawmi madrasa-based Islamist group, yesterday called for fair investigations and exemplary punishment over child abuse allegations and condemned some people’s attempts to take the law into one’s own hands.

In a statement, its Ameer Allama Muhibbullah Babunagari and Secretary General Sajedur Rahman said proper investigations, administrative action and punishment were essential to maintaining law and order.

Calling child sexual abuse a longstanding problem affecting schools, madrasas and other settings, they stressed the importance of children’s safety and psychological well-being.

Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) yesterday demanded stronger child protection in madrasas, impartial investigations, legal action and effective Sexual Harassment Prevention Committees in all educational institutions.

It warned that actual cases could be higher, as children often remain silent due to fear, stigma or pressure.

“No child should fear the people responsible for their care and education. When a child reports abuse, we must listen, take immediate action and ensure their safety,” said MJF Executive Director Shaheen Anam, urging parents to encourage disclosures and assure children of support.

Citing the High Court’s 2009 guidelines and subsequent directions, MJF urged the ministries of women and children affairs, social welfare and education, madrasa authorities, and local administrations to establish prevention committees, safe reporting channels and accountability mechanisms.

Salma Ali, adviser to the Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers’ Association, welcomed the protests but called them belated.

“Protests alone are not enough. We also want to see what the government does in response,” she told The Daily Star.

Many cases, particularly in rural areas, never reach police or courts due to stigma, fear of further victimisation and local settlements, she said.

Concerned about abuse of boys at residential madrasas, particularly orphans who often remain silent, she recalled an earlier case involving an 11-year-old pregnant madrasa student.

She sought coordinated monitoring by the ministries of religious affairs, education, home, law, and women and children affairs and local authorities, alongside police training, effective investigations, safe accommodation, legal aid and rehabilitation.

“Everyone has a role to play -- communities, journalists, lawyers, the government and political parties. Without collective action, these incidents cannot be prevented,” she said.

Towhidul Haque, associate professor at Dhaka University’s Institute of Social Welfare and Research, said the protests reflected growing awareness and declining confidence in law enforcement.

Previously, accused teachers often escaped accountability through quiet settlements, apologies or promises not to reoffend, he said.

“Had the authorities taken legal action from the beginning, people would not have felt compelled to take the law into their own hands.”

Warning that mob violence was no solution, he urged stronger institutional oversight, better teacher-student relationships, modern teaching practices and changes in institutional attitudes and culture.

(Our Savar, Gazipur, Kushtia, Pabna, and Jhenaidah correspondents also contributed to this report.)

The jailing of 85 people following a raid on a senior police officer’s house in Purbachal last week has raised questions over the evidence behind their convictions and the circulation of their photographs and videos.

The Detective Branch (DB) detained 85 people, including 59 men and 26 women, in a raid on a house owned by Additional DIG Abdullah Al Jahir in Police Housing-1 on October 20.

According to DMP sources, Special Metropolitan Magistrate Assaduzzaman of DMP’s Uttara Division sentenced all of them the same day in summary trials.

The 59 men were each given one month in jail and fined Tk 1,000, while the 26 women received 15-day terms and fines of Tk 500 each.

The detention, trials, and circulation of the detainees’ images have left their families traumatised. Most families contacted by The Daily Star declined to discuss the incident, saying they were shocked. Only one agreed to speak, on condition of anonymity.

Rajib Hossain (not his real name), whose son was among those detained, said his son, a DJ, had previously attended a birthday programme at the same house on invitation.

This time, however, police detained him with the others on allegations of drug consumption and had him sentenced by a special court without any test to establish whether he had consumed drugs or alcohol, Rajib alleged.

Rajib said he had visited his son at Dhaka Central Jail in Keraniganj, where he was told that none of the detainees had undergone such tests.

“When there was no test, how did they establish that they had consumed drugs or alcohol?” he asked.

Asked about this, DB chief Shafiqul Islam told The Daily Star yesterday that the detainees had been arrested on allegations of drug consumption and disorderly conduct before being punished by a special court.

Asked under which law they were punished, he said the relevant magistrate would be able to explain the legal basis for the sentences.

However, a DB official closely involved in the operation, speaking on condition of anonymity, said police had proceeded under Section 36(5) of the Narcotics Control Act, 2018.

The provision allows imprisonment of up to one year and a fine for anyone who, after consuming alcohol or while under the influence of an intoxicating substance, disturbs public peace or engages in annoying behaviour, or drives a vehicle while intoxicated.

Rajib also questioned the circulation of photographs and videos of the detainees and the circumstances in which some were allegedly made to show their faces.

“Can the DB circulate such videos and photographs? Under what authority were they made to show their faces? My son is not a criminal. Why should he be publicly portrayed like this?” he said.

He further alleged that his son and the other detainees might have become victims of internal disputes within the police.

“We heard from several police sources that the additional DIG had internal issues that led to the raid,” he claimed.

Supreme Court lawyer Sara Hossain questioned the legal basis for the punishments, saying attending a DJ party or dancing was not a criminal offence.

“What exactly is an ‘illegal DJ party’? How did the party become illegal?” she told The Daily Star. “It’s not a crime in itself to go to a party, let alone a DJ party.”

If the detainees were punished under the Narcotics Control Act, she said, the authorities must establish the alleged offences through evidence.

“The offence is not dancing or being at a DJ party. If the allegation is that they consumed intoxicating substances and disturbed public peace, what evidence was produced?” she asked.

Criticising descriptions of the gathering as an “illegal DJ party” and the participants as being involved in “antisocial activities”, she said music and dancing were part of the country’s culture.

“How can enjoying music or dancing be treated as a crime? Are they committing an offence because they were listening to modern music? This is absurd,” she said.

Sara also questioned why the detainees were filmed and their photographs and videos circulated, including footage recorded before their convictions.

“Why were they filmed at that stage, when nothing had been proved against them? What was the justification?” she asked.

She said the convictions did not resolve questions over the circulation of the images if the proceedings themselves were unlawful, and questioned whether publishing the images served any public interest.

“We certainly need operations against crime, but every operation must be carried out according to the law,” she said.

Supreme Court lawyer Barrister Faran Mohammad Araf also questioned the manner of the raid, saying police appeared to have acted on information without obtaining a warrant.

He said one of the most relevant legal guidelines, interpreting article 32 of the constitution, concerned protecting detainees’ dignity at the time of apprehension.

“Even when making an arrest, law enforcers must respect an individual’s dignity and personal liberty. They cannot publicly expose or humiliate someone or turn them into an object of ridicule,” he told The Daily Star.

He said existing laws and directives concerning the media favoured protecting the dignity, privacy, and rights of accused persons rather than subjecting them to public humiliation.
author: Tousif Kaium Arafat Rahaman

body:
A half-day blockade of roads and waterways in Rangamati and Khagrachhari yesterday disrupted transport services as protesters demonstrated against alleged attacks, baton charges and vandalism during Thursday’s blockade at Ujo Bazar in Sajek, Rangamati.

Called by the Chhatra Janata Sangram Parishad, the blockade began in the morning and ended at noon.

In Rangamati, protesters blocked the Rangamati-Khagrachhari road with logs and set fires at Sapchhari Khamar Para and Kutukchhari Dharmaghar. They also brought out a procession from Kutukchhari Half Bazar to Dharmaghar.

Vehicular movement on the Rangamati-Khagrachhari road remained suspended throughout the morning, while traffic continued on the Rangamati-Chattogram road despite the blockade in Betbunia.

Md Yusuf, joint general secretary of the Rangamati-Chattogram Bus-Minibus Workers Union, said bus services on the Rangamati-Khagrachhari route resumed after noon, although passenger numbers were low.

In Khagrachhari, no long-distance buses departed, although some auto-rickshaws operated in the town.

Protesters burnt tyres at Chengi Bridge, Swonirbhar and Jorabridge in Guimara, while felled trees blocked the Chattogram-Khagrachhari road at Sapmara.

Khagrachhari Sadar Police Station OC Md Kay Kislu said police escorted overnight buses from Dhaka into town. Some vehicles stranded in Ramgarh were instructed to enter Khagrachhari after noon.

[Our correspondents from Rangamati and Khagrachhari contributed to this report]

A court in Netrokona has sent two men to jail following their arrest in connection with the alleged gang rape of a 37-year-old woman in Durgapur upazila.

The two accused, Hasibul Hasan, 25, and Hafizul Hasan Rabbi, 26, were produced before the Netrokona Senior Judicial Magistrate Court on Thursday evening, which ordered them to be sent to jail.

Durgapur Police Station Officer-in-Charge Khandakar Shaker Ahmed confirmed the matter to The Daily Star today.

The arrestees are residents of the Madhyabazar area under Durgapur municipality. Another accused, Ashik Mia, 26, remains absconding.

Police said locals had initially attempted to settle the matter through an arbitration. After receiving information about the incident, police went to the area and arrested two of the accused.

According to the case statement, the woman, who works at a garment factory in Dhaka, returned to her village home in Durgapur on October 19. Her husband works as a mason in the capital.

Her maternal cousin had also come to Durgapur. He visited the woman's house around 10:00pm on October 21. Following dinner, they slept in separate rooms.

A Gazipur court today sent two people to jail in a case filed over the alleged rape of an eight-year-old boy by a teacher at a residential Qawmi madrasa in the district.

The Gazipur Senior Judicial Magistrate Court passed the order after police produced Md Oliullah Islam, 23, the teacher, and Mohammad Mizan, 38, of the madrasa's governing body, before the court this afternoon, said Gacha Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Golam Rabbani.

Police conducted a drive and arrested the two individuals yesterday.

Earlier, the victim's mother filed a case with Gacha Police Station against Oliullah, Mizan, and one Md Abdul Quddus Sheikh, 45, in connection with the incident, said the OC.

According to the case statement, around 1:00am on October 10, the accused teacher woke up the victim, a Class 3 student, while he was sleeping along with other residential students in the residential block of the madrasa and took him to the madrasa's storeroom and raped him. The teacher took the child to the same place at around 1:30am on October 11 and 3:00am on October 12 and raped him again. The accused also threatened to beat the child if he told anyone about the incidents, according to the case statement.

When the child went home on October 13, his mother noticed signs of abuse while giving him a bath and after confronting him, the victim revealed the incidents to his mother.

She later filed a complaint with the respective police station which was recorded as a case.

UK High Court has frozen a £15 million London apartment linked to Anisuzzaman Chowdhury Ronny, brother of Bangladesh’s former land minister Saifuzzaman Chowdhury Javed, after anti-corruption investigators alleged that the property was connected to embezzlement, corruption, fraud and money laundering, reports the Financial Times.

UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) secured the order this week to prevent the sale or transfer of the luxury apartment near Regent’s Park after Anisuzzaman failed to explain the source of funds used by his company to purchase it, the report said.

In a witness statement presented by the NCA, an investigator described the arrangements surrounding the property’s ownership as “deliberately opaque”, it added.

At a hearing on Thursday, the court was told that Anisuzzaman had been served with an unexplained wealth order last year, requiring him to demonstrate that the apartment had been purchased with legitimate funds. Under UK anti-corruption laws, failure to provide a satisfactory explanation creates a legal presumption that the property was acquired through unlawful conduct.

NCA investigator said the agency suspected that the property derived from unlawful conduct, including “embezzlement, corruption, fraud and money laundering”.

The witness statement also cited forged signatures attributed to former US president Richard Nixon, former UK prime minister David Cameron and US singer Chris Brown on documents, describing their use as evidence of a “cavalier” attitude towards fraud.

According to the investigator, Anisuzzaman transferred the company holding the apartment’s title to a third party in September 2025 for a nominal £1, through a structure allegedly designed to return control of the property to his wife and two daughters.

UK Land Registry records show that Anisuzzaman purchased the Regent’s Park apartment through his company, Ronny 42 Limited, in 2023 for £12.4 million.

The High Court in in London heard that the company was renamed PNN UK Properties after its transfer to the third party.

In a written submission, NCA lawyers described the transaction as “nothing more than an arrangement of convenience” intended to facilitate the refinancing of loans secured against the apartment from Singapore’s DBS Bank.

Although the stated price for the company’s shares was £1, the NCA said the total value of the share sale was £14.95 million.

The agency added that the DBS loan had not been refinanced and that the Singaporean bank was pursuing repossession of the apartment following a loan default.

Justice Karen Steyn ruled that there was a good arguable case that the property represented the proceeds of crime and granted the freezing order. She also allowed an exception permitting landlord possession proceedings to be brought.

Anisuzzaman’s solicitors told the court that they did not oppose the freezing order.

Speaking to the FT, he said he had decided, on legal advice, not to contest the NCA’s application but denied any unlawful conduct. He said he would vigorously defend any civil recovery proceedings brought by the agency and demonstrate that the allegations against him were untrue.

He also denied disguising the property’s ownership, saying it had been “transparently disclosed” to the NCA. He added that he would “thoroughly defend any defamatory statement against my wife and children who have nothing to do with this”.

NCA investigator’s witness statement, dated July, said Anisuzzaman was in the UK and had used the apartment as his principal residence.

According to the FT report, Saifuzzaman, who served as Bangladesh’s land minister, and members of his family built a property portfolio worth $295 million between 1992 and 2024.

Following the ouster of the Sheikh Hasina-led government in August of 2024, the interim administration led by Muhammad Yunus sought to trace overseas assets it alleged had been purchased with money taken out of Bangladesh during her period of authoritarian rule.

In June 2025, the NCA froze properties linked to Saifuzzaman worth about £185 million as part of an ongoing civil investigation. The agency also secured an unexplained wealth order against the former minister, his wife and related companies that month.

Saifuzzaman had taken out hundreds of mortgages from British bridging-loan specialist Market Financial Solutions, which collapsed this year amid allegations of fraud.

Anisuzzaman previously told the FT that he had “no business relation” with his brother.

A local Jubo Dal activist was hacked to death by unidentified criminals in Satla area of Wazirpur upazila in Barishal on Friday night.

The deceased was identified as Kawsar Hawlader, 37.

A group of armed criminals attacked Kawsar when he along with Rashed Amin and several other Jubo Dal activists were standing on a bridge around 9:30pm, said Wazirpur Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge Rakibul Islam.

Kawsar and Rashed jumped into the water beneath the bridge and sheltered in a nearby house.

The attackers then entered the house by breaking open the door and hacked Kawsar, said the OC.

He was taken to Kotalipara Upazila Health Complex where doctors declared him dead. Rashed was also injured in the attack, he added.

A crude bomb exploded near the Office of the Assistant Commissioner of Police in the Ramna Zone, commonly known as the old Ramna Police Station, in Dhaka tonight.

The explosion occurred around 8:00pm, said Sheikh Zahidul Islam, deputy commissioner of Ramna Division.

“No casualties were reported,” he added.

Police are investigating the incident.

Police have filed a GD over an altercation between lawmaker Rumeen Farhana and Sarail Police Station OC Manzur Kader Bhuiya.

The GD was filed on Thursday night, but the matter came to light on Friday evening, the OC said.

Police were preparing a list of those who accompanied the lawmaker to the police station. Further action would be taken following instructions from senior police officials, he added.

Rumeen, who represents Brahmanbaria-2, comprising Sarail, Ashuganj and part of Bijoynagar, went to the OC’s office with her supporters around 7:30pm on Thursday.

They argued over alleged security lapses and police misconduct. Videos of the heated exchange later circulated on Facebook.

Her supporters alleged that tensions had been building for days, as the OC had not responded to calls from Rumeen and her personal assistant.

They also claimed that the lawmaker had sought security but did not receive it. Rumeen later said she had gone to the police station to discuss allegations against the OC.

Five Bangladeshis have been charged in Canada over an alleged immigration fraud scheme involving 243 temporary resident visa applications for 209 Bangladeshi nationals. Investigators found fake documents and false statements in the applications.

According to a news release issued by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) on October 22, four of the accused appeared at the Valleyfield courthouse in Quebec that day. They are Rashel Mirza, Mohammed Aminul Islam, Md Mudassar Alam Bhuiyan and Kazi Nafeez Alam.

The fifth accused, Md Rakibul Hassan, is reportedly in Bangladesh. An arrest warrant has been issued against him.

The investigation began after the CBSA conducted a compliance operation at a private residence in Mercier, Quebec, on July 3, 2024, with officers and representatives of the town's police and fire departments. The agency identified indications of possible violations of Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and formally launched an investigation in August that year.

Investigators found that 243 temporary resident visa applications had been submitted for 209 Bangladeshi nationals seeking to visit Canadian citizens presented as their hosts.

According to the CBSA, an elaborate scheme had allegedly been established to help the applicants obtain visas using fraudulent documents and false statements.

On June 3, 2025, investigators executed four search warrants at locations in Quebec and Ontario. Documents, computer equipment and other evidence gathered during the searches pointed to the involvement of the five accused in the alleged scheme.

Given the scale and complexity of the investigation, the CBSA focused on 79 of the 243 applications that it considered most probative.

The accused face three charges -- conspiring to organise or facilitate the entry of people into Canada; knowingly inducing, aiding or abetting people to misrepresent or conceal material facts in immigration applications; and knowingly inducing, aiding or abetting people to violate Canada's immigration law.

The charges have yet to be validated by the court, and the allegations have not been proven. Judicial proceedings are ongoing.

Immigration specialists warn that submitting forged documents or false information in a Canadian visa application can result in the application being refused and a ban on entering Canada for at least five years, as well as further legal complications, the press release said.

CBSA advised applicants to verify the accuracy of all information and supporting documents before submitting an application, adding they should also remain aware of the information submitted on their behalf by representatives or consultants and avoid placing blind trust in anyone who guarantees a visa.

Brahmanbaria-2 MP Rumeen Farhana has alleged that a digitally altered image depicting her as the Hindu goddess Durga was circulated on Facebook to incite religious tensions after she attended Durga Puja celebrations in Ashuganj, Brahmanbaria.

In a post on her verified Facebook account this afternoon, Rumeen criticised those who "mistake the cultivation of hatred for religious devotion."

Referring to sexual violence, corruption, fraud and the denial of others’ rights, she argued that such wrongdoing should be judged on moral grounds rather than excused under the guise of piety.

She added that showing respect for people of other faiths should not be seen as a religious failing.

Rumeen visited several Durga Puja mandaps in Ashuganj upazila, and photographs of her visits were shared on social media.

When contacted by The Daily Star, Rumeen said, “Circulating AI-generated images to incite division and hatred is not just an insult to me; it is insulting to people of all religions. Portraying a person as a goddess is insulting to all religions.”

The National Citizen Party (NCP) has restructured its central convening committee, retaining Nahid Islam as convener and Akhter Hossen as member secretary, while announcing a 16-member Political Council and a revised list of 195 central committee positions.

The party’s office cell confirmed the committee lists today.

Under the revised structure, Nasiruddin Patwary and Hasnat Abdullah have been appointed senior joint conveners, while Sarjis Alam and Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain have been named senior joint member secretaries. The committee also includes 24 joint conveners and six joint member secretaries.

There are 36 top leadership positions, 28 divisional and diaspora organisational posts, 54 subject-specific secretarial posts, 19 assistant secretaries and 58 general members.

The party has appointed an organisational secretary and an assistant organisational secretary for each of its 10 regional units: Dhaka North and South, Chattogram North and South, Rajshahi, Rangpur, Sylhet, Khulna, Barishal and Mymensingh. The diaspora unit has eight office-bearers, comprising four organisational secretaries and four assistant organisational secretaries.

Political council

The 16-member Political Council has been drawn from the central committee.

Besides Nahid and Akhter, its members are Patwary, Hasnat, Sarjis, Asif, Advocate Abdullah Al Amin, Ariful Islam Adeeb, Dr Atiq Mujahid, Abdul Hannan Masud, Ali Ahsan Junaid, Sarwar Tushar, Akram Hossain, Saleh Uddin Sifat, Dr Mahmuda Alam Mitu and Nusrat Tabassum.

Former senior joint convener Samantha Sharmin has been appointed a joint convener, while former senior joint member secretary Nahida Sarwar Niva has been made a joint member secretary. Neither has been included in the Political Council.

The revised structure also abolishes the posts of chief coordinator, chief organiser and spokesperson.

In the divisional organisational structure, Saifullah Haider and Abdullah Mohammad Hossain have been appointed organisational secretaries for Dhaka North and Dhaka South respectively.

Assistant secretaries have also been appointed to various portfolios.

Opposition Leader and Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Shafiqur Rahman today expressed concern over tourists stranded amid a blockade in Sajek, a popular tourist destination in Rangamati, and an exchange of gunfire between the army and an armed hill group.

In a post on his verified Facebook page at around 2:15pm today, Shafiqur asked, “What is happening centring on Sajek in Baghaichari upazila of Rangamati district?”

“Instead of chasing false intelligence, clear steps need to be taken in this regard based on accurate intelligence,” he said.

“No one has the right to play with the lives of ordinary citizens. Take appropriate action while there is still time,” he added in the post.

Sajek Gano Odhikar Rakkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association have been staging protests with three demands, including the removal of armed members of the Parbatya Chattogram Jana Samhati Samiti (JSS-Santu Larma) from Sajek Valley.

As part of the movement, the two organisations announced an indefinite blockade of the Sajek tourist road yesterday afternoon and urged tourists to leave the area.

The district administration later temporarily closed Sajek Valley to tourists over safety concerns and instructed visitors to leave the area by 4:00pm today.

The blockade began at 6:00am today, with protesters placing logs across the road at several points, including Ujo Bazar. Around 8:30am, they stopped a convoy of tourists returning from Sajek Valley, leaving about 2,350 people stranded.

At around 11:30am, the army exchanged gunfire with an armed hill group in the Ujo Bazar area while evacuating tourists stranded by the blockade, police said. The situation returned to normal about an hour later.

The Inter-Services Public Relations Directorate (ISPR) also confirmed the exchange of gunfire.

Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan has been hospitalised at Evercare Hospital in Dhaka with respiratory and cardiac complications.

"He was admitted to the hospital on Wednesday night with breathing difficulties and heart problems," Women and Children Affairs Minister Professor Dr AZM Zahid Hossain said after visiting Moyeen Khan at the hospital this afternoon.

"He is receiving treatment under close medical observation, and his condition is more stable today than yesterday," Zahid said.

Moyeen Khan, also a member of the BNP Standing Committee, is being treated under the supervision of Evercare Hospital physicians Dr Atikur Rahman, Dr Ziaul Haque and Dr Zafar Iqbal.

BNP Acting Secretary General Advocate Ruhul Kabir Rizvi visited the minister at the hospital this evening and spoke with the doctors about his latest condition.

Moyeen Khan's family has sought prayers from people across the country for his speedy recovery.

Seven Qawmi madrasa-based political parties have decided to work together under the guidance of Hefazat-e-Islam, although their leaders are reluctant to describe the initiative as a political alliance at this stage.

The decision was taken at a meeting chaired by Hefazat Secretary General Sajidur Rahman at Makhjanul Ulum Madrasa in Khilgaon yesterday. Three representatives from each of the seven parties and three Hefazat leaders attended the meeting.

The parties are Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis, Khelafat Majlis, Islami Andolan Bangladesh, Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam, Islami Oikya Jote (Razi), Nezame Islam Party and Bangladesh Khelafat Andolon.

Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis Secretary General Maulana Jalaluddin Ahmad told The Daily Star, “The seven like-minded Islamic parties have decided to move forward together for the welfare of the country, its people and Islam. We will work together on programmes, statements and take positions on various issues.”

He said the parties had previously worked under a common platform and now wanted to resume cooperation along similar lines.

“The decision by these seven parties to work together does not mean that parties belonging to other political alliances will have to leave those alliances. No such decision was taken at today’s meeting,” he said.

According to meeting sources, a 21-member liaison committee, comprising three representatives from each of the seven parties, has also been formed.

Jalaluddin Ahmed said the next meeting, scheduled for December 5, would discuss future activities in greater detail.

The parties took the decision at a meeting chaired by Hefazat Secretary General Sajidur Rahman at Makhjanul Ulum Madrasa in Dhaka’s Khilgaon this afternoon. Three representatives from the seven parties and three Hefazat leaders attended the meeting.

The parties are Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis, Khelafat Majlis, Islami Andolan Bangladesh, Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam, Islami Oikya Jote (Razi), Nezame Islam Party and Bangladesh Khelafat Andolon.

Confirming the development, Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis Secretary General Maulana Jalaluddin Ahmad told The Daily Star, “The seven like-minded Islamic parties have decided to move forward together for the welfare of the country, its people and Islam. We will work together on programmes, statements and taking positions on various issues.”

He said the parties had previously worked under a common platform called "Like-minded Islamic Parties" and now wanted to resume cooperation along similar lines.

Jalaluddin said the initiative would not require any party to leave its existing political alliance.

“No party will be required to leave another alliance as a condition for joining this initiative. Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis is also part of the 11-party alliance by its own decision,” he added.

Hefazat was represented by its nayeb-e-ameers Abdul Awal and Ayub Babunagari.

Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar yesterday accused the government of creating an opportunity for the Awami League to return to politics through “wrong politics”.

“Do not push the country into a fire of anarchy and instability. By creating unrest and pushing the streets towards confrontation, you are giving the Awami League a chance to return to politics through your own wrong politics,” he said.

Porwar made the remarks at the 49th founding anniversary programme of Bangladesh Labour Party as the chief guest at the party’s central office in Segunbagicha, Dhaka.

Speaking at an event in Rajshahi on Tuesday, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman alleged that the ousted regime and a section of the opposition were conspiring to destabilise the country. Citing intelligence reports, he claimed that the AL was sending money from abroad to a political party in Bangladesh to create unrest.

Jamaat-e-Islami’s central publicity department issued a press release containing Porwar’s remarks.

The Jamaat leader said the government had become embroiled in disarray within seven months because the BNP had failed to move away from political immaturity and short-sighted leadership.

Chittagong University (CU) unit of Jatiya Chhatra Shakti has been suspended by the organisation’s central committee less than three months after its full-fledged committee was announced.

The decision came amid allegations of organisational inactivity, the president’s inability to devote regular time to the organisation, and controversy surrounding a vice-president’s stay at a mess linked to Bangladesh Chhatra League, according to sources.

The suspension was announced in a statement signed by Sardar Nadim Mahmud Shuvo, office secretary of Jatiya Chhatra Shakti, today.

According to the statement, the decision was taken by the organisation’s central president Abu Bakar Majumder and general secretary Tahmid Al Muddassir Chowdhury. The suspension will remain in force until further notice.

Since the committee was announced, the unit has not been seen carrying out any significant organisational activities, sources said. Meanwhile, the detention of one of its vice-presidents from a mess linked to Chhatra League also drew attention.

Asked about the matter, Abdullah Al Mahathir, the outgoing president of the university unit, said he was nearing the end of his student life and was completing his master’s degree.

“I am unable to devote regular time to the organisation. So, I am considering formally stepping down and handing over responsibility to new leadership,” he said.

Earlier, concerns had been raised over the unit president’s inactivity. This year, vice-president Tanvir Ahmed Sabbir was detained by police after staying at a mess linked to Chhatra League.

On July 27 this year, the central committee approved a 52-member full-fledged committee for the CU unit. Abdullah Al Mahathir was named president, Md Ismail general secretary, and Md Ulfatur Rahman organising secretary.

Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar today accused the government of creating an opportunity for the Awami League to return to politics through “wrong politics”.

“Do not push the country into a fire of anarchy and instability. By creating unrest and pushing the streets towards confrontation, you are giving the Awami League a chance to return to politics through your own wrong politics,” he said.

Porwar made the remarks at the 49th founding anniversary programme of Bangladesh Labour Party as the chief guest at the party’s central office in Segunbagicha, Dhaka.

Speaking at a public event in Rajshahi yesterday, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman alleged that the ousted regime and a section of the opposition were conspiring to destabilise the country. Citing intelligence reports, he claimed that the Awami League was sending money from abroad to a political party in Bangladesh to create unrest.

Jamaat-e-Islami’s central publicity department issued a press release containing Porwar’s remarks.

Criticising the government, the Jamaat leader said the government had become embroiled in disarray within seven months because the BNP had failed to move away from political immaturity and short-sighted leadership. He also accused the government of trying to shift the blame for its own misdeeds onto the opposition.

Porwar said it was the opposition’s responsibility to expose the government’s misdeeds and partisan appointments before the nation. However, whenever the opposition criticised the government, it was accused of creating instability, he said, adding that such behaviour amounted to following the path of fascism.

He further alleged that the BNP government was following the same path as the Awami League, which used to accuse opposition figures of conspiring against the state. The government was also trying to silence the opposition, he claimed.

Instead of blaming the opposition for labour unrest and instability in industrial areas, the government should address workers’ concerns over rising prices of essential commodities and demands for minimum wages in line with market prices, Porwar said.

He said the opposition had not enforced any hartal or blockade, set fire to vehicles or engaged in vandalism while campaigning for the implementation of the referendum verdict. The opposition had been holding peaceful programmes to prevent instability in the country, he said.

Porwar urged the government to accept the referendum verdict, in which 70 percent of voters voted “yes”, and implement the constitutional reform proposals through discussions with the opposition.

Bangladesh Labour Party Chairman Mostafizur Rahman Iran chaired the programme, which was also addressed by senior leaders of the 11-party alliance.

Porwar called on people to join the third phase of the long march on October 31 along the Dhaka-Khulna-Jashore-Jhenaidah-Kushtia route.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman yesterday inspected Mongla Port, the Sundarbans and the site of a proposed economic zone in Bagerhat, raising hopes for investment and development in the southwestern region.

He left Dhaka by helicopter around 9:00am and flew over parts of the Sundarbans, including Hiron Point, before landing at Nalian Secondary School ground in Dakop upazila of Khulna around 10:30am.

The premier then travelled by waterway to BNS Mongla, a Bangladesh Navy facility, where he met Navy, port and local administration officials.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, state ministers Aninda Islam Amit and Shaikh Faridul Islam, Whip Rakibul Islam and other senior officials were present.

After the meeting, Tarique inspected Mongla Port’s jetty facilities and operations before visiting the proposed economic zone site planned by the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority (BEZA).

He returned to Dhaka by helicopter around 5:00pm.

BNP leader Hafizur Rahman Tuhin said the port’s development, the proposed LNG terminal near Akram Point and the economic zone would boost the regional economy. He also called for improved jetty facilities and dredging.

Md Julfikar Ali, general secretary of the Mongla Port Berth and Ship Operators’ Association, said floating storage regasification unit facilities would support energy supplies and industrial growth.

Sheikh Sahed Ali Robi, president of the Bagerhat Chamber of Commerce and Industry, called for regular dredging to maintain the port channel’s navigability and modernisation of customs services.

State Minister Faridul said industrialisation and investment centred on Mongla Port would create jobs and improve livelihoods, including for people affected by climate change.

He said coordinated development of the port, economic zone and Sundarbans tourism would help turn the region into a major trade and investment hub.

Islami Andolan Bangladesh and Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis have expressed concern over the prime minister’s remarks alleging an understanding between the ousted autocrat and an opposition party.

At a public rally in Rajshahi on Tuesday, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said intelligence reports indicated that the ousted autocrat was providing money from across the border to a particular political party that was trying to create instability in the country.

Responding to the remarks, Islami Andolan Bangladesh Secretary General Maulana Gazi Ataur Rahman said that if the government possessed such intelligence, it could not fulfil its responsibilities merely by making statements at public rallies or urging people to remain vigilant.

Administrative action must be taken against those involved, Gazi Ataur said in a statement issued today.

He questioned why legal action had not been taken against those involved if the prime minister had specific intelligence about such an understanding.

“As a political party opposed to autocracy and as conscious citizens, we want to know what steps have been taken based on the specific intelligence received by the prime minister,” he said.

In a statement, Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis Secretary General Maulana Jalaluddin Ahmad demanded a detailed explanation from the prime minister over his claim.

Jalaluddin said the prime minister’s remarks were deeply concerning.

“If there is specific evidence to support the statement, it must be made public and legal action must be taken against those concerned. The prime minister cannot discharge his responsibility merely by making a speech at a public rally,” he said.

Jalaluddin said, “If the prime minister’s statement is true, the question is why action has not been taken against those accused despite the existence of intelligence information. And if there is no specific basis for the statement, why make such a sensitive allegation and try to mislead the public? The prime minister must provide a clear explanation.”
